articles.title: In Ruby, Objects Don't Have Methods. How Method Lookup Actually Works.
articles.description: A visual deep dive into Ruby's object model under the hood. Why objects store state but zero methods, how hidden eigenclasses work, and the real method lookup path.
articles.body_html:
Ask almost any developer how object-oriented programming works, and they will describe the same textbook picture: an object bundles data and methods together into a single unit.

In Ruby, you hear this idea reinforced constantly under the slogan: "Everything is an object."

You create a string, call .upcase on it, and it feels completely natural to assume that the string object owns that method. You create a user object, call .save, and assume .save lives inside your user.

Except that is not how Ruby works at all.

In Ruby, objects contain zero methods.

If you inspect an instance down at the C source code level in CRuby (MRI), you discover something surprising: an object stores its instance variables, a set of internal flags, and a pointer to another structure. It does not contain a single line of method code, nor does it contain a method table.

Where do methods actually live? How does Ruby know what to execute when you type user.greet? And what actually happens when you define a method on a single specific object?

To truly master Ruby, you have to look beneath the syntactic sugar and understand the mechanics of Ruby's object model: method tables, the hidden eigenclass, and the ancestry ladder.

The First Surprise: Objects Store State, Classes Store Methods

Let us look at a simple Ruby class:

class User
  def initialize(name, email)
    @name = name
    @email = email
  end

  def greet
    "Hello, I am #{@name}"
  end
end

user = User.new("Alice", "alice@example.com")

When Ruby evaluates User.new, the virtual machine allocates a heap structure called an RObject.

Inside this RObject, Ruby stores two things:

  1. An array of instance variables: @name set to "Alice", and @email set to "alice@example.com".
  2. An internal pointer named klass, pointing directly to the User class object.

Notice what is missing from user: the greet method is nowhere to be found.

Methods in Ruby live exclusively inside classes (represented internally as RClass).

The User class contains a hash table called m_tbl (the method table). When you define def greet, Ruby writes an entry into User's method table mapping the symbol :greet to its compiled bytecode body.

When you call user.greet:

  1. Ruby does not look inside user.
  2. Ruby follows user's internal klass pointer to the User class.
  3. Ruby searches User's m_tbl for :greet.
  4. It finds the method and executes it in the context of self = user.

This separation is what makes Ruby memory-efficient. You can instantiate one hundred thousand User objects, and all one hundred thousand share the exact same method table inside User. The instances only hold their personal instance variables.

The Mystery of Singleton Methods

Now consider this famous Ruby feature: you can add a method to just one individual object without affecting any other instance of that class.

str1 = "hello"
str2 = "world"

def str1.shout
  upcase + "!!!"
end

str1.shout #=> "HELLO!!!"
str2.shout #=> NoMethodError: undefined method 'shout' for "world":String

This raises a fascinating puzzle:

  • We already know that objects cannot hold methods. So :shout cannot live inside str1.
  • :shout cannot live inside String, because then str2 would also have access to it.

If objects cannot hold methods, and the class cannot hold this method, where on earth does shout live?

Ruby solves this by doing something brilliant: it quietly invents an invisible class on the fly.

The moment you define a method on str1, Ruby creates an anonymous, hidden class called an eigenclass (officially referred to as a singleton class).

Ruby then performs an architectural sleight of hand:

  1. It intercepts str1's internal klass pointer and repoints it to this new singleton class (#<Class:str1>).
  2. It sets the superclass of the singleton class to String.
  3. It places the :shout method inside the singleton class's method table.

When you call str1.shout, Ruby follows the klass pointer into #<Class:str1>, finds :shout, and runs it.

When you call str1.upcase, Ruby looks in #<Class:str1>, does not find :upcase, follows the superclass pointer up to String, finds :upcase, and runs it.

To regular code, the singleton class is almost completely transparent. You do not see it in str1.class (which still reports String). But you can prove it exists with Ruby's reflection methods:

str1.singleton_class
#=> #<Class:#<String:0x00007fffa80c2180>>

str1.singleton_methods
#=> [:shout]

"Class Methods" Do Not Exist

Once you understand eigenclasses, one of the biggest myths in Ruby evaporates: there is no such thing as a "class method".

Developers frequently write code like this:

class Post
  def self.recent
    # query recent posts
  end
end

Tutorials often say: "This defines a class method on Post."

In languages like Java or C++, a static method is a distinct language construct. But in Ruby, Post is not a special entity. Post is simply an object. It is an instance of the class Class.

Post.class
#=> Class

Because Post is an object, writing def Post.recent or def self.recent is doing the exact same thing as writing def str1.shout: it is defining a singleton method on an object.

The :recent method does not live in Post, and it does not live in Class. It lives in Post's own private eigenclass (#<Class:Post>).

In Ruby, there are only instance methods. What we call "class methods" are merely instance methods living on the singleton class of a class object. The entire language operates on one single, unified rule.

The Complete Method Lookup Ladder

When you type receiver.message, what is the exact order Ruby follows to find the code?

Ruby does not search haphazardly. It walks an exact, deterministic ladder called the ancestors chain. The first match it encounters executes immediately.

Here is the exact step-by-step lookup path:

  1. The Receiver's Eigenclass: If the object has any singleton methods, they get first priority.
  2. Prepended Modules on the Eigenclass: Any module added with prepend sits in front of the eigenclass.
  3. The Receiver's Class: The standard class where ordinary instance methods reside.
  4. Prepended Modules on the Class: If a module was prepended to the class, its methods override the class's own methods.
  5. Included Modules on the Class: If a module was included in the class, it is inserted directly above the class in the hierarchy.
  6. Superclasses (and their modules): Ruby climbs to the parent class, checking its prepends, own methods, and includes.
  7. Object, Kernel, and BasicObject: The root ancestors shared by virtually all Ruby objects.

What Happens When Nothing Matches?

If Ruby climbs all the way to BasicObject without finding a matching method, it does not immediately raise an error.

Instead, Ruby walks back down to the starting receiver and starts the entire search again from step one, this time searching for a method named method_missing.

Because Kernel provides a default implementation of method_missing that raises NoMethodError, your program only crashes if no intermediate module or class intercepts it.

This two-pass search is what powers Ruby's famous metaprogramming libraries, from ActiveRecord dynamic finders to OpenStruct.

How "Everything Is an Object" Runs Fast: Tagged Pointers

If every number, boolean, and nil value in Ruby is an object with methods, how does Ruby avoid grinding to a halt allocating heap memory for basic math?

If you run:

total = 0
1_000_000.times { |i| total += i }

Does Ruby allocate one million RObject structs on the heap?

In CRuby, the answer is no, thanks to an internal optimization called Tagged Pointers (Immediate Values).

On a 64-bit operating system, memory addresses are aligned to 8-byte boundaries. That means the lowest 3 bits of any valid heap pointer are always 000.

CRuby takes advantage of these unused bits. When a 64-bit value represents a small integer (called a Fixnum), Ruby shifts the integer left by one bit and sets the lowest bit to 1:

value = (integer << 1) | 1

When the Ruby virtual machine sees a value with the lowest bit set to 1, it knows: "This is not a heap pointer. This is the raw integer itself."

Similarly, CRuby reserves specific bit patterns for singleton values:

  • false is represented as 0x00
  • nil is represented as 0x08
  • true is represented as 0x14

When you call 42.even?, Ruby does not inspect a heap block. It detects the tagged pointer, looks up the method in the Integer class method table, and executes the code without a single byte of memory allocation or garbage collection overhead.

You get the clean conceptual purity of "everything is an object" combined with the efficiency of primitive register arithmetic.

The Mental Shift

Ruby's object model is often described as complex, but under the surface, it is remarkably minimal:

  1. Objects store state and an internal klass pointer. They never hold methods.
  2. Classes store methods and an internal super pointer. They never hold instance state.
  3. Singleton methods live in invisible eigenclasses, seamlessly spliced into the lookup chain.
  4. Class methods are just singleton methods on class objects, because classes are objects too.
  5. Tagged pointers preserve pure object semantics without sacrificing performance.

Once you see the object model through this lens, Ruby metaprogramming stops feeling like black magic. Concepts like class_eval, instance_eval, prepend, and singleton classes become predictable mechanical tools that follow one coherent set of rules.

When you first learned Ruby, what was the quirk in its object model that made you stop and rethink how programming languages work? And if you have used eigenclasses in production, what was the problem you solved with them?

References:

  • Ruby Core Documentation: Class and Object
  • Ruby Core Documentation: Object#singleton_class
  • Pat Shaughnessy: Ruby Under a Microscope (In-depth analysis of MRI C structures)
  • Paolo Perrotta: Metaprogramming Ruby 2 (The definitive guide to Ruby's object model)

articles.title: Building an Open-Source Support Tool That Turns Your Docs into Reusable Knowledge
articles.description: I spend a good part of my day working with the community at CopilotKit, answering questions in...
articles.body_html:
I spend a good part of my day working with the community at CopilotKit, answering questions in Discord, GitHub, and Slack, helping people get unstuck, and pointing them to the right resources.

I started building answerLoops to help me with that work. As it took shape, I added integrations for more platforms so other teams could use it in their communities too.

It’s open source, and I’m building it in public.

Explore answerLoops on ⭐️ GitHub

A big part of the work has been deciding how knowledge gets into the system. Some answers are in the docs. Others come out of a support conversation or are things someone on the team just knows.

For an agent to use those answers, the team needs a straightforward way to save them, review them, and keep them current. That’s what I’ve been building into the knowledge base.

Answering the question is only part of the work

A question comes in. You find the relevant documentation or resource, figure out how it applies to that person’s setup, and write a reply.

During that conversation, you might discover something the docs don’t cover. A missing setup step, a confusing default, or a workaround that deserves its own article.

You resolve the question, but that useful detail stays buried in the conversation. When someone else asks, the team has to find it again.

I want answerLoops to help with both parts: preparing a useful answer now and saving what the team learns for future questions.

What answerLoops does

answerLoops is an open-source AI support tool that brings questions from Discord, Slack, GitHub, Telegram, and other connected channels into one dashboard. It uses your knowledge base to help prepare answers.

For knowledge-based replies in the ticket pipeline, a Mastra agent generates a draft and a separate agent scores its confidence and whether it fully answers the question. Automatic replies are off by default. When enabled, answers that meet the configured criteria can be sent automatically; other drafts remain available for human review.

There’s also an embeddable website chat widget built with CopilotKit and connected to a Mastra support agent. Visitors can ask questions directly, with published knowledge-base articles supplied as reference material.

The widget supports richer responses, including step-by-step guides, quick replies, callouts, link cards, and contact options.

But the quality of those answers depends on the information available to the agent. That’s why much of the recent work has been on the knowledge base.

Add the answer that isn’t in your docs

Sometimes you don’t need to import a documentation site. You just need to write down something the agent should know.

An owner or admin can open Knowledge Base → Manage and use Write an answer by hand:

  1. Enter a question or title.
  2. Write the answer or context.
  3. Click Add to knowledge base.

For example, a customer might ask whether changing a configuration requires a restart. Someone on your team knows the answer, but it isn’t documented anywhere.

The article is published and indexed when it’s saved, making it available for subsequent questions. There’s no draft step in this form, so the answer should be suitable for customers to read.

Adding an article doesn’t retrain the model. It gives the agent another reference to retrieve when a relevant question comes in.

Articles added this way appear under Added by hand in the Knowledge coverage tab.

It’s a small feature, but it gives the person with the answer a direct way to improve what the agent knows.

Bring in the knowledge you already have

You can also populate the knowledge base from existing content:

  • Documentation URLs: import a page or crawl a documentation site.
  • Files: upload PDF, DOCX, Markdown, text, or CSV files.
  • GitHub: sync Markdown and MDX files, with optional syncs when changes are pushed to the default branch.
  • Notion: connect pages and databases your team wants to use.

Notion content imports unpublished. Your team can inspect it before making it available for customer-facing answers, and that publishing choice is preserved across syncs.

The manual-entry form sits alongside these sources. If an answer already exists in your docs, import it. If it only exists in someone’s head, write it down.

Turn a resolved ticket into reusable knowledge

Closing a ticket helps the person who asked. Turning that resolution into a knowledge-base article makes the explanation available for future questions.

The Promote to KB action lets an owner or admin turn that ticket’s question and answer into a knowledge-base article.

Before promoting it, check that the answer applies beyond the original conversation. Remove account-specific details and make the explanation useful to someone encountering the same problem later.

This matters for the website widget in particular. Its retrieved reference material comes from published KB articles, rather than raw resolved tickets.

Promoting an answer gives it a place in the shared knowledge base where the widget can find it.

Let customer questions help you decide what to write

You won’t know every gap in your documentation ahead of time.

The Review tab captures questions that weren’t covered by the available knowledge. On hosted plans, this queue is available on Pro and above.

A usable draft can come along as a starting point. If there isn’t one, the item is marked No usable answer, and someone can write it.

Owners and admins can edit the question and answer, then choose Approve and add to knowledge base. If the item shouldn’t become an article, they can reject it instead.

Nothing in the queue becomes searchable customer-facing knowledge until it’s approved.

When the same question comes in again, its counter increases instead of creating another copy. The most-asked questions appear first.

If several people ask about the same setup step, that’s a useful signal about what your knowledge base is missing. The queue gives your team a question to work from and a place to review the answer before publishing it.

Go from a knowledge gap to a new article

The Knowledge Gaps page provides another view of where support needs attention.

It surfaces tickets with low-confidence answers, tickets that need a person, and resolved questions without a covering KB article.

Repeated questions are grouped with an Asked N times badge, so you can see recurring topics without reading every ticket separately.

The + KB action opens the manual-entry form with the ticket’s question and any existing answer filled in. Review the text, add the article, and it’s linked back to the ticket to close that gap.

You don’t have to leave the question behind and start a blank document somewhere else.

Check what the agent can actually find

Importing a document doesn’t tell you whether it will help with a particular question.

The Knowledge coverage tab shows articles grouped by source, including whether they’re live, unpublished, or not searchable.

There’s also a Try a customer question field. It runs the same lookup the website widget uses and shows which articles match—or that nothing covers the question.

After adding an answer, try the original customer question and a few variations. Does the lookup find the article you just wrote? If it doesn’t, you have something concrete to investigate before judging the generated reply.

This checks retrieval, not whether every generated reply will be correct. You still need to review the answers themselves. But it gives you a way to investigate whether the intended information is being found.

The KB is the source of product knowledge your team maintains for the agent. If no article matches, the assistant can fall back to general knowledge, which may not fit your product. Finding those gaps and adding the right material is part of maintaining it.

See which articles are being used

answerLoops also tracks article usage.

It counts when an article is supplied as context for an answer that is actually produced, including website replies and ticket drafts.

The distinction matters: this means the article was given to the agent, not necessarily that the final reply quoted it.

Searches and simulations don’t increase the count.

Together with the coverage view and repeated-question counts, this helps you understand what information is being retrieved and where more work might be useful.

Where CopilotKit and Mastra fit

I work in DevRel at CopilotKit, so part of building answerLoops is putting the tools I work with into a product and sharing what I learn.

Mastra runs the agents behind the support drafts and website conversation, including the chat agent’s thread memory.

CopilotKit provides the foundation for the custom widget interface. The application connects that interface to the agent and supplies the relevant knowledge-base context.

The product also has its own workflows around those pieces: importing sources, reviewing unanswered questions, publishing articles, and handling staff actions on tickets.

Those workflows are where the team gets to improve the information the agent uses. Someone can spot a missing answer, write it, publish it, and check whether a future question retrieves it.

That’s become a much bigger part of answerLoops as I’ve kept building.

Try it and tell me what’s missing

I started this to help with my own community work. I’m sharing it so other developers and support teams can try it in theirs.

The code and setup instructions are on GitHub. You can explore how retrieval, the review queue, and the integrations work, or run answerLoops yourself. The knowledge-base documentation walks through the workflows in this article.

If it looks useful, give the repo a ⭐️. If you try it, tell me what worked and what got in your way.

New to contributing to open source? Reach out—I’d be happy to help you find a place to start.

Where does your team keep the useful answers that haven’t made it into the docs yet?

articles.title: 2 Agent Skills Every Frontend Developer Should Try
articles.description: I love to try out new agent skills. Anything that can help me be more productive I'm all for. Today I...
articles.body_html:
I love to try out new agent skills. Anything that can help me be more productive I'm all for. Today I found two new ones I want to share with you.

First one is Impeccable. Impeccable took a plain, AI-built website and gave it a design. It wasn't bad at all! Diagram Design took that same site and drew a diagram of how it works! Both install with one command, and both work with basically any coding harness. I used Kiro in my demos but you can use whatever you like.

I made a video walking through both if you'd rather watch:

Prerequisites

  • An agent that supports Agent Skills. I use Kiro, but Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex work too.
  • Node.js, so you can run npx.
  • A frontend project to try them on. Mine is a small website about cats.

Finding skills

I found both skills on Skill Leaderboard, which ranks skill repos by GitHub stars. You can filter by compatible agent, so I set it to Kiro. Skills are like recipes that work across most coding harnesses, so you'll usually be fine without the filter. Some repos are easier to install in one agent than another, though, and the filter saves you from finding that out the hard way.

Stars measure popularity. I cared more about what fits my own projects, so I picked the two that match what I build most, which is websites.

Before you install anything, read the SKILL.md and any scripts it pulls in. A skill is instructions and scripts that run with your agent's permissions, so check it the same way you'd check an npm package.

1. Impeccable

Impeccable is a design skill that started from Anthropic's frontend-design skill and builds on top of it. It has UX planning, a set of design commands like critique, polish, and audit, and it asks you a lot of questions.

To test it, I had Claude Opus 5.5 vibe code a site called the Great Cat Color Census. You spot a cat in the wild, click "Spotted one," and the counts and leaderboard update. Out of the box it came with a blocky card style and some hover animations. It looked okay. I don't think it looked bad, but it was pretty generic.


The default design Claude Opus 5.5 came up with.

Install it from your project root:

npx impeccable install

Then run init inside your agent:

/impeccable init

Init looks through the project, asks about anything it can't work out on its own, and writes a PRODUCT.md with what it learned. After that I asked it to make the site much nicer using its styles. It came back with five or six design directions. I picked the sticker one.


The sticker direction from Impeccable. Same features, new design.

It has basically the same features as before, and you can still summon a random cat. It looks a lot more polished, with extra animation and cats that look like peel-off stickers. The font gives it a Cat in the Hat feel. I don't have a very particular taste for frontend design, and I still like this version better. If you're a designer, tell me in the comments whether you agree.

A good way to use Impeccable is to have it build several of its directions on separate Git branches. Then you can run each one and compare them side by side before you commit to a look.

2. Diagram Design

Diagram Design draws diagrams as one self-contained HTML and SVG file. It supports 45 diagram types, from architecture diagrams and flow charts to radar charts and Venn diagrams. The screenshots in the repo don't do it much justice.

Install it with the skills CLI:

npx skills add cathrynlavery/diagram-design

I asked it for a diagram of the same cat site and didn't say what to diagram. There's no backend, so I wasn't expecting much. It picked the visitor flow. A visitor clicks, an action runs change() or reset(), the counts update, and the derived stats feed the left and right pages. It also shows the save and load path to localStorage, and it even carried over the pink styling from the site.


The diagram Diagram Design made from the cat site, open in Kiro.

It's a simple diagram, but I like the style, and I can see myself using it on my next project. It's also handy when you open a code base with little documentation. Ask it for a few diagrams before you start reading the code.

The rest of the list

I haven't spent much time with the other popular skills yet. These are my notes so far.

Ponytail gives your agent the personality of the laziest senior dev in the room. In its README, you show him fifty lines, and he says nothing and replaces them with one. The goal is less code and fewer tokens. In Kiro it loads as an always-on ruleset, so you don't get its slash commands.

Caveman makes the agent answer tersely to cut token usage. I haven't seen much savings myself. Someone in a Reddit thread on the top Kiro skill repos said it raised their token usage, even though the research the repo cites says otherwise.

Addy Osmani's agent skills add a spec, plan, build, and test workflow to your agent. Kiro has specs built in, but if your tool doesn't, this or Superpowers is how I'd add spec-driven development.

I haven't tried UI UX Pro Max or Graphify yet, even though they're near the top of the list.

If you build on AWS, look at the Agent Toolkit for AWS. It's our set of skills and MCP servers for working with AWS from your agent, and it's free on GitHub.

Wrap up

If you build websites, Impeccable is the one I'd install first. Diagram Design is right behind it, especially when you're new to a code base.

I'm thinking about testing whether Ponytail and Caveman save tokens in Kiro. Leave a comment if you want to see that, and tell me which skills you're using.

articles.title: My OSS Projects: dets
articles.description: This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or...
articles.body_html:
This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or helped to grow – with the back story, what they do well, where they struggle, and what's next. Previous parts: AngleSharp, MAGES, Piral, Electron.NET, Netpack and Picard.js.

We are getting close to the end of this series: only two projects left. Today's is one of the quieter ones – it has no logo that anyone remembers, no conference talk, and no hype. What it has is a job it does reliably: dets, a TypeScript declaration file bundler.

It started as a helper for Piral, and it grew up a bit since then.

What is dets?

dets generates a single .d.ts file from your TypeScript code. You tell it what the entry points are, and it produces one self-contained declaration file with only the API you care about – and no dependency on other declaration packages.

That's useful in two situations:

  1. You want to selectively expose an API (and not everything that happens to be exported somewhere).
  2. You want a self-contained declaration file that you can ship, copy, or publish as-is.

The package description says exactly this, in five words: "A TypeScript declaration file bundler". It's MIT licensed, lives at github.com/FlorianRappl/dets, and – to my own surprise – is downloaded several thousand times per week.

The back story: a shell for plugins

To explain why dets exists I have to explain how Piral thinks about the world.

In Piral, the app shell is a plugin-enhanced app: it loads micro frontends (pilets) at runtime and gives them an API to integrate with it – register a page, add an extension, access shared data, and so on. For micro frontend teams to be productive they need that shell on their machine: to debug locally, and to build and check their code against what the shell really offers.

And since the shell comes with an API, the natural thing (at least in the web world) is to ship TypeScript declarations for it. Then the IDE can tell you what is available, and your build tool can complain if your assumptions are wrong. (Compile errors are better than production errors. Always.)

"But the shell is written in TypeScript – don't we get that for free?"

That was my first thought, too. It is also wrong, for a few reasons:

  • The app shell is an application, not a library. Most of what's in there is not meant for micro frontends.
  • The API for the micro frontends is only a subset of the app shell.
  • The shell brings nothing of that API to the runtime. The types are compile-time only. There is no object you can point at and say "this is the API".

So what you'd need is a declaration file that describes just the part that is relevant. And that's something TypeScript's own tsc --declaration does not give you: it emits one declaration file per source file, mirrors your internal structure, and happily references everything.

The failed attempts

First I tried the obvious: take the plugin API definition of the app shell and feed it to the various type bundling tools out there. It did not go well. Whatever I tried either failed outright or produced vast amounts of ill-formatted garbage.

At some point you have to accept the pattern: type bundling – or type extraction in general – is not a solved problem.

One weekend, one experiment

That's when I spent a weekend on an experiment: Can I use the TypeScript compiler API to actually infer the types and re-build a .d.ts with only the API I care about?

It turns out: yes. But not easily.

Along the way I learned an awful lot about how TypeScript infers and enriches type information, and how its internal model is built up – symbols, declarations, types, flags, merging, aliases… you name it. Things that you never need to think about when writing TypeScript become very present when you try to print it.

The main catch, however, was the API itself. It was meant to be internal. At some point the TypeScript team wanted (and even tried out) a plugin story with real API users. But it seems they found it easier to leave it undocumented and keep it their safe space. Whoever uses the API should be prepared for surprises in future versions.

So dets became a tool that stands on an unstable foundation by design. That sounds worse than it is – it just means that keeping up with TypeScript versions is a feature of this project, not an accident (more on that below – including a look at what's inside).

Getting started

Install it as a dev dependency:

npm i dets --save-dev

(npx dets or a global install work, too.) Then point it at your entry module:

dets src/index.ts --name foo --files "src/**/*.ts" --out dist/index.d.ts

The options you will meet most often:

Option What it does
entry (positional) The entry-level modules to consume. This is what you should reach for in most cases.
--name The module name. If omitted, it's taken from the nearest package.json.
--files The files TypeScript gets to see.
--imports Packages whose imports should stay external (not bundled in).
--ignore Respect @ignore comments and drop those members (default: true).
--module-declaration Wrap the output in a declare module "name" { … } block (default: true).
--out The output path (default: ./dist/index.d.ts).

There are also lower-level options (--types, --apis) for selecting types by file and interfaces by InterfaceName:FilePath – handy when the API is defined as an interface, but not exported from a single entry point (hello, app shells).

From code

If you want to integrate dets into your own tooling, there is a programmatic API, too:

import { generateDeclaration } from 'dets';
import { writeFileSync } from 'fs';

const content = await generateDeclaration({
  name: 'my-app-shell',
  root: process.cwd(),
  files: ['src/**/*.ts'],
  types: ['src/api.ts'],
});

writeFileSync('dist/index.d.ts', content);

generateDeclaration returns the content; writing it somewhere is up to you. (If you need finer control, setupVisitorContext, fillVisitorContextFromApi and fillVisitorContextFromTypes give you the building blocks – e.g. to say "use this exported object as the API".)

Shaping the output

Bundling everything that is reachable is the easy part. The interesting part is controlling what ends up in the file.

Special comments

dets understands a few comment tags:

export interface Foo {
  bar: string;
  /**
   * Internal – should not be visible for consumers.
   * @ignore
   */
  secret: number;
}
  • @ignore drops the member from the output (can be disabled via --no-ignore).
  • @dets_preserve keeps an @ignored member and removes only the tag itself – useful if something is hidden in one context but needed in another.
  • @dets_removeprop and @dets_removeclause are for merged interfaces: they remove named properties or extends clauses from the combination. (Declaration merging is a powerful TypeScript feature, and a splendid source of surprises.)

Plugins

For everything else there are plugins. They hook into the phases shown above (before-init, before-process, after-process, before-stringify) and can modify the model before it is printed. There are two styles: a classic one – an object with type, name and run(context) – and a modern one, where a single plugin implements multiple lifecycle hooks:

const plugin = {
  name: 'my-plugin',
  'before-init'(context) {
    // prepare something
  },
  'after-process'(context) {
    // adjust the collected types
  },
};

There is also a built-in createExcludePlugin(['some-module']) to drop whole modules from the output (declaration merges on other modules still apply).

Under the hood: the TypeScript compiler API

Time to open the hood. If you have never touched the compiler API, here's the mental model that made everything click for me.

Three layers: text, syntax, meaning

When TypeScript processes your code, it builds up information in layers:

  1. The parser turns text into a tree of nodes – the AST. A node knows what is written and where (ClassDeclaration, Parameter, StringKeyword, …). That's purely syntactic. A node has no idea what Foo in x: Foo actually is.
  2. The binder walks the tree and creates symbols. A symbol is the semantic identity behind a name: "there is a class called SomeClass, with the members value and foo". Symbols point back to their declarations (the nodes). And here is the key trick: multiple declarations can share one symbol. That's how declaration merging works – an interface and a class with the same name, two interfaces in two files, a namespace that extends a function. In the AST these are unrelated nodes; in the symbol table they are one thing.
  3. The checker computes types from symbols and nodes – lazily, on demand, and cached. It resolves imports and aliases, follows export { a as b }, and infers what nobody wrote down.

This second part – symbols and types – is what I mean by the "semantic tree" that sits next to the AST. It is why TypeScript can do what it does: completions, refactorings, error messages, and .d.ts emit all depend on it. The syntax alone is not enough: export * from './foo' tells you nothing about what is exported until something resolves ./foo, finds its symbols, and merges them in.

Nodes vs. symbols vs. type nodes vs. types

The naming is confusing, so let's pin it down using a class from dets' own test fixtures:

  • Node (ts.Node): one piece of syntax. Everything you can point at in the source.
  • Type node (ts.TypeNode): a node that is a type annotation – string, Foo<T>, A | B, { x: number }. It is syntax: it exists only if someone wrote it. [1, 2] has no type node, but it very much has a type.
  • Symbol (ts.Symbol): the named entity the binder created. Carries flags (Class, Interface, Alias, …), its declarations, and its members / exports.
  • Type (ts.Type): what the checker knows. foo() above returns string, even though that's written nowhere.

The reason this matters for dets: the output is syntax. A .d.ts is text, so we need type nodes to print – but for inferred things, the checker only gives us types. The bridge is checker.typeToTypeNode(type), which converts semantics back into syntax. That one function is the reason dets works at all for code like foo() { return this.value; }.

A tiny example of the three APIs working together (this is not dets code, just the shape of things):

import ts from 'typescript';

const program = ts.createProgram(['src/index.ts'], { strict: true });
const checker = program.getTypeChecker();
const file = program.getSourceFile('src/index.ts')!;

ts.forEachChild(file, (node) => {
  if (ts.isClassDeclaration(node) && node.name) {
    // syntax: what is written
    console.log(ts.SyntaxKind[node.kind]); // "ClassDeclaration"

    // meaning: the symbol behind the name
    const symbol = checker.getSymbolAtLocation(node.name)!;
    console.log(symbol.declarations?.length); // 2+ if merged

    // knowledge: the type (and back to a printable type node)
    const type = checker.getTypeAtLocation(node);
    const typeNode = checker.typeToTypeNode(type, undefined, ts.NodeBuilderFlags.NoTruncation);
  }
});

From options to program

Where does the program come from? In dets, generateDeclaration (in src/commands.ts) is the conductor. Roughly:

  1. Collect the source files (files, the files of the apis, and the types entries – minus whatever is excluded).
  2. Create a ts.Program with a small, fixed set of compiler options: JS allowed, esModuleInterop, ESNext modules, React JSX – and Bundler module resolution if the installed TypeScript is 5.3 or newer, Node10 otherwise. (That's the "keeping up with TypeScript versions" part, in one line.)
  3. Fill a visitor context with the exports that should be part of the result – from an exported object (apis) or from all exports of a module (types).
  4. Run the plugin phases around the visitor: before-init → create the visitor → before-process → processQueue() → after-process → before-stringify.
  5. Stringify the result into the final declaration.

Everything interesting happens in step 4.

The most important file: src/input/node.ts

If dets has a heart, it is src/input/node.ts. It contains the DeclVisitor: the class that walks declarations and converts them into an intermediate model (plain objects describing interfaces, classes, aliases, functions, …) that the output stage can print.

A work queue, not a recursive walk

The visitor starts with the exports from the context and puts them in a queue. processQueue drains the queue; every declaration goes through processNode, which is basically a big dispatcher:

// simplified
processNode(node: ts.Node) {
  this.processed.push(node); // remember first, handle later

  if (ts.isTypeAliasDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeInContext(node, () => this.getAlias(node));
  } else if (ts.isFunctionDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeInContext(node, () => this.getFunctionDeclaration(node));
  } else if (ts.isInterfaceDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeExportedInterface(node);
  } else if (ts.isClassDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeInContext(node, () => this.getClass(node));
  } else if (ts.isEnumDeclaration(node)) {
    this.includeInContext(node, () => this.getEnum(node));
  } else if (ts.isExportDeclaration(node)) {
    // export { a as b }   vs.   export * from './x'
  } else {
    this.printWarning('type', node); // we don't know this one (yet)
  }
}

The key design decision: a reference is a name, not a body. When a type mentions another type (foo: Bar), the visitor does not descend into Bar right there. It enqueues the declaration of Bar and puts a reference-by-name into the model. That has two nice consequences:

  • Every declaration is emitted exactly once, no matter how often it's referenced.
  • Cyclic types (A references B, B references A) terminate for free.

That is also how "tree shaking" for types works: if nobody references it from the entry, it never gets into the queue.

Walk the nodes, ask the checker only when needed

Most of the file is getTypeNode: a long chain of ts.isX guards that routes each type node to a handler – unions, literals, arrays, type references, indexed access, keyof/readonly, mapped types, conditional types, function and constructor types, infer, intersections, tuples (and named/optional/rest members), typeof queries, template literal types, and imports. Keywords like string or unknown are handled as constants.

Interestingly, the file does not switch on ts.Type flags. dets mostly walks the syntax and only reaches for the checker when the syntax doesn't say enough. The typical case is a missing annotation:

// simplified
getReturnType(node: ts.SignatureDeclaration) {
  if (node.type) {
    return this.getTypeNode(node.type); // written down – just use it
  }

  // not written down: ask the checker what it inferred
  const signature = this.checker.getSignatureFromDeclaration(node);
  const returnType = this.checker.getReturnTypeOfSignature(signature);
  const typeNode = this.checker.typeToTypeNode(returnType, undefined, ts.NodeBuilderFlags.NoTruncation);
  return this.getTypeNode(typeNode);
}

(NoTruncation is important – by default TypeScript abbreviates large types with ..., which is great for hover tooltips and terrible for a declaration file.)

The same pattern shows up for variables (annotation, then initializer, then inferred type), default exports, and typeof queries on imported values, which are expanded into synthetic interfaces.

Where symbols come in: merging, aliases, names

Symbols earn their keep in three places.

Declaration merging. When dets handles an interface, it asks the checker for the type's symbol and collects all interface declarations of that symbol – skipping those that come from imported packages. Heritage clauses, members and type parameters of all declarations are combined (without duplicates) into one interface. Classes do the same with interfaces that share the class symbol. That's the scenario where @dets_removeprop and @dets_removeclause come in handy.

Export aliases. For export { a as b }, the visitor resolves the specifier to the actual symbol (getExportSpecifierLocalTargetSymbol, getAliasedSymbol) and then renames the result.

Names. Two different declarations may have the same name – from different files, or an import that collides with a local type. All declarations of one symbol share one name, and a collision gets a ___N suffix:

// simplified
createName(name: string) {
  const prefix = `${name}___`;
  const taken = new Set([...this.names.values()].filter((n) => n === name || n.startsWith(prefix)));
  return taken.size > 0 ? `${prefix}${taken.size}` : name;
}

Yes, a type called Foo___1 in your declaration file is slightly ugly. It is also correct, which beats the alternative.

Externals

Not everything should be bundled in. If a type comes from an external package, it's not copied: includeInContext checks whether the symbol belongs to a package (via a helper called getPackage), and if so, it becomes an import instead of part of the model. That's what the --imports option controls.

When it doesn't know

Whatever the visitor does not understand ends up in a warning (Could not resolve type at position …) rather than a crash. The log levels (0.8.0) let you decide how loud that should be. When you see such a warning on your code: that's a new test case waiting to happen.

How testing works in dets

A tool whose job is to produce exact text from arbitrary code has a natural test strategy: feed it small pieces of code and compare the output to the expected text.

The setup is refreshingly boring:

  • Fixtures. tests/assets/ contains ~150 small TypeScript files: class1.ts, interface1.ts, merge1.ts, enum1.ts, react1.tsx, vue1.ts, … Each one isolates a single feature or bug.
  • A helper. runTestFor(name, options) calls the real generateDeclaration with sensible defaults: module name test, the assets folder as root, and the fixture as both files and types. Options can be overridden per test.
  • Tests. About 30 test files (classes.test.ts, merge.test.ts, tuple.test.ts, typeof.test.ts, …), run with Vitest. Each test runs the helper on a fixture and compares the result to a template literal.

Here is what the simplest one looks like. The fixture:

export class SomeClass {
  public constructor(private value: string) {}

  foo() {
    return this.value;
  }
}

And the test – abbreviated (the repo has the exact expected text), with the expectation being the full text of the generated declaration:

import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { runTestFor } from './helper';

test('should be able to handle exported classes with constructor', async () => {
  const result = await runTestFor('class1.ts');
  expect(result).toBe(`declare module "test" {
  export class SomeClass {
    private value;
    public constructor(value: string);
    foo(): string;
  }
}
`);
});

Note the foo(): string; – that is the inferred return type from the checker, making a round trip through typeToTypeNode.

A few things I like about this approach:

  • It's a real end-to-end test. No mocking of the compiler. Every test creates an actual program and uses the actual checker – which is exactly where the bugs live.
  • Exact comparison (toBe). No normalization of whitespace. The declaration file is a product; indentation and order are part of it.
  • Every bug gets a fixture. Titles like "should treat readonly fields correctly (issue 55)" are a diary of the project. The 14 tests in classes.test.ts alone cover constructors, modifiers, generics (explicit and implicit), implemented interfaces, React classes from externals and bundled in, static members, accessors, readonly, and class/interface merging.
  • Real-world typings. The helper can also point at the typings of piral-base and piral-core (the original use case!), and the dev dependencies read like a who's who of typings: React, Redux, React Router, styled-components, Vue. If it can handle those, it can handle your code.

The CI (GitHub Actions) runs the tests and the build on every push to main or develop and for pull requests to develop. A push to develop publishes a pre-release to npm under the next tag (with the run number in the version); a push to main publishes the real thing – with provenance – and creates the git tag. The build script even runs dets on itself: the shipped dist/index.d.ts is bundled by dets, with typescript as the external import. If the tool can't describe its own API, that's a red flag.

One more detail from the changelog: in 0.16.5 the tests moved from Jest to Vitest – a good reminder that even a test suite is just another dependency to keep alive.

The changelog: a tour of 1.0

With about 60 changelog entries, the CHANGELOG tells the story better than I could. I find it easiest to read in four themes.

Teaching it the language

The early releases are a march through the language: 0.1 brought classes, generics and constructor calls (and extends/implements came in 0.1.5). 0.2.0 was the big one: a rewrite of the engine for better resolution and accuracy, with support for dynamically placed imports and destructuring. 0.3.0 added interface merging resolution, tuples and enums, 0.3.2 accessors (get/set) and readonly. Later highlights: overloads and the satisfies operator (0.12), named tuples (0.11.2, 0.12.3), triple-slash directives (0.14.1), the spread operator (0.16.3), and in 1.0.0 optional tuple entries.

Control

Once the output was right, people wanted to shape it. 0.8.0 added log levels with custom log providers. 0.9.0 introduced @ignore handling and the @dets_preserve, @dets_removeprop and @dets_removeclause tags. 0.10.0 added lifecycle plugins (and declaration merging for externals). 0.12.0 added the module-declaration option, 0.14.0 a modern plugin API with multiple lifecycle hooks (and made the API async), and 0.18.0 the excluded option.

Keeping up with TypeScript

The thread that runs through the whole history. TypeScript became a peer dependency in 0.4.0, 0.7.0 added TypeScript 4, 0.11.0 added guards for older versions, 0.13.0 added TypeScript 5 and dropped TypeScript 3, and 0.14.1 fixed TypeScript 5.3 not considering externals. 1.0.0 finally improved the version independence – and fixed importing types from hidden submodules.

Housekeeping

Bundling moved from ncc to esbuild (0.13.0), Node 14, 16 and 18 were dropped step by step (0.15, 0.17, 0.18) – the minimum is Node.js 20 – the tests moved to Vitest (0.16.5), and publishing now uses npm's trusted publishing via GitHub Actions (0.18.0). Plus a long tail of "fixed X" entries, many triggered by issue reports: dots in names (0.16.5, thanks to @longlostbro), readonly in constructors (0.17.0), and more.

And then, finally, 1.0.0: the version number that says "this has been around long enough".

Where dets shines

  • API subsets. Exactly the use case from above: take a big application, expose only the part that's meant for others.
  • One file. Combining all the .d.ts files of a library into a single one – especially if the library is bundled and compressed anyway. It's tidy.
  • Controllable. Special comments, plugins and a programmatic API let you adjust the result without post-processing strings.
  • TypeScript-version independent. Over the years it moved from TypeScript 3 through 4 to 5 and the 1.0.0 release improved version independence further.

Where dets struggles

Let's be honest:

  • It stands on internals. I use TypeScript's compiler API – the part that's intentionally under-documented and not stable. A TypeScript release can (and sometimes does) break things. The changelog is full of entries like "fix for TypeScript 5.3" for exactly this reason.
  • Type extraction is hard. Complex type-level programming, odd declaration merging, and exotic constructs may need a plugin or a comment hint to come out right.
  • Small project. There are a few dozen stars and a small group of users. It does one thing, and there's not much of a community around it.
  • Documentation. The README covers the options, but it is not a book. For the more advanced scenarios the best documentation is the source and the tests.

dets today

In the Piral world, dets is used in two places:

  • For the emulator typings of Piral: the app shell's API is turned into a declaration file that ships with the emulator, so micro frontend developers get completion and type checks locally.
  • For libraries in the ecosystem: combining all the .d.ts files into one – the nicest fit for libraries that are bundled / compressed anyway.

Beyond that, the npm download counter shows about 7,000 downloads per week (12–18 October 2026: 7,215) – more than I'd have guessed for a tool that started as an internal helper.

What's next: TypeScript 7

The big question mark: TypeScript 7. The compiler is being ported to a native implementation, and with that, the future of the TypeScript API as we know it is still to be determined. I am sure that an API will return at some point – too many tools depend on it, and it would be strange to not offer a way to build on top of the compiler.

Until then, the plan is simple: we stay with TypeScript 6 (or 5) and are happy to keep on bundling. If dets needs an adaptation once the new API shapes up, I'll make it – and write about it, probably.

  • 📦 npm: dets

  • MAGES
  • Piral
  • Electron.NET

One more project to go after this one – and it's a big one. Stay tuned!

articles.title: I broke an Elementor site on purpose, then built a tool to find the bugs
articles.description: BeeLadybug 0.5 adds CSS hunt: a zero-dependency overlay that tells you WHY a WordPress page looks broken — !important rules, overflow causes, invisible text, click blockers and stretched images.
articles.body_html:
The night I broke my own site

I'm 53, I work in a factory, and in the evenings I build things in vanilla JavaScript.

Lately I've been looking at freelance WordPress jobs. Almost every one of them says the same thing: "Elementor site, layout is broken, fix it."

So I did something a bit crazy. I took an empty test site, installed Elementor, and asked an AI to break it for me — 5 hidden CSS bugs, packed into an encoded script so I couldn't just read the answer.

Then I tried to find them.

It was humbling. The page looked wrong, but the console said nothing. Of course: CSS doesn't throw errors. A bad rule is still a valid rule, so the browser applies it silently. That's exactly why clients say "everything moved and I don't know why."

I found the first bug the slow way — DevTools, Styles panel, unchecking rules one by one until I saw it:

.elementor-section, .e-con { margin-right: -60px !important; }

Twenty minutes for one line. I thought: there must be a faster way.

So I built one: CSS hunt

🐞 BeeLadybug is my zero-dependency debugging overlay. You paste one line in the console and it attaches to any page — WordPress dashboards, Elementor pages, mobile viewports. It already showed element size, classes, display type, FPS and memory.

Version 0.5 adds a new mode: CSS hunt (press F6).

When you hover an element, it tells you what's wrong with it:

  • !important rules that match the element, and where they come from (<style> inline or the stylesheet URL)
  • Overflow causes: which element actually leaves the viewport, plus negative margins
  • Invisible text: color: transparent, opacity: 0, or text the same color as its background
  • Click blockers: what sits on top of the element's center, including fixed ::before / ::after on html / body
  • Stretched images: natural ratio vs rendered ratio, when object-fit is fill

Press S to scan the whole page. Click a line and the element gets a red outline.

The hard part: telling the truth without noise

My first version was technically right and practically useless.

One card overflowing the screen produced ten red lines: the card, its article, its p, its h2… All "overflowing", because they inherited it. A fixed overlay blocking clicks? One warning per element underneath it.

A real developer doesn't want ten alarms. They want the culprit.

So the scan now:

  1. Reports the cause, not the containers. An ancestor is skipped if a descendant overflows by the same amount (±2px).
  2. Groups by cause. Instead of 12 lines you get: 
▾ body::after blocks clicks on 12 elements
    div.elementor-element-629ef32
    img#1301
    summary.elementor-element-3925463
    …
  1. Separates bugs from info. Red = bug. Grey = info, like unreadable sheet: fonts.googleapis.com (cross-origin stylesheets can't be read — that's a browser rule, not a problem on the page).
  2. Keeps the log calm. Hover and DOM-mutation lines are hidden unless you turn on verbose mode (F3). Each issue is logged once per element every 5 seconds. Press P to pin the panel on an element and read it in peace.

The real test

The demo page bugs are easy — I wrote them. The real test was the broken Elementor page, with Elementor V4 "atomic" widgets, Google Fonts, Altervista ad scripts and all the usual mess.

Result: CSS hunt found the click blocker, the negative margin overflow, the invisible button text and the stretched image on a live page I didn't build the bugs for.

Try it

Open any page, press F12, paste this in the console:

import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bee-ladybug@0.5.3/src/index.js')
  .then(({ BeeLadybugCore, WebDOMAdapter, CSSAdapter }) => {
    const bee = new BeeLadybugCore();
    new WebDOMAdapter(bee, { root: document.body }).attach();
    new CSSAdapter(bee).attach();
    window.bee = bee;
  });

Then press F6, hover, and press S.

No build step, no framework, no dependencies. Just vanilla JavaScript.

What I learned

  • CSS bugs are silent. The console won't help you. You need to look at computed styles and geometry.
  • The right answer is not enough. A debugging tool must point to the cause, or it's just another wall of text.
  • Breaking things on purpose is the best teacher. I recommend it to anyone who wants to do WordPress fixes for clients.

I'm still learning. If you try CSS hunt on a broken page and it misses something, tell me in the comments — that's how the next version gets better.

🐞 npm: bee-ladybug

articles.title: A 9.2 unauthenticated RCE in PHP: the audit, the patch window, and the offline switch
articles.description: CERT-EU says sites that can't patch should go offline: two 9.2 flaws in PHP itself, unauthenticated RCE, every version since PHP 5 possibly affected. The audit, the watch, and the offline switch — runnable receipts for the emergency window.
articles.body_html:
An EU cyber agency is telling websites they may need to be taken offline. Not patched later. Not monitored. Offline. The runtime that powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento and most of the shared hosting internet has two 9.2-rated flaws — unauthenticated remote code execution — and the patch lands today at 14:00 GMT.

On Wednesday, the PHP security team releases fixes for two critical vulnerabilities rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale. Reuters reports what the agencies and vendors are saying around it — and the short version is that this is as serious as web emergencies get:

  • CERT-EU: the 9.2 rating indicates a risk of unauthenticated remote code execution — code running on your server without login. Their guidance: prepare for immediate patching, and those unable to patch should take affected sites offline.
  • ACSC (Australian Cyber Security Centre): identify every PHP system in your environment, prepare to patch, monitor for exploitation. Currently not aware of active exploitation — currently.
  • GoDaddy: the flaws could allow code execution over the internet — data theft, defacement, full system compromise.
  • Huntress: "PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood."
  • Scope: all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected. Details, affected versions and fixed releases publish when the patch drops at 14:00 GMT today.

If that sounds dramatic for a language release, it is — and it should be. This is not a plugin bug or a framework edge case. It is the runtime itself.

Why this breaks the grading system

I grade controls on this blog in levels: what a control sees, who wrote it, what it survives. A Level 1 control is visible and bypassable; the quiz-hook post was one. The level below that is the ground the levels stand on: the runtime. Your WAF rules, your input validation, your hardening checklist — every one of them is PHP executing your defense. An unauthenticated RCE in PHP is an attack on the level that decides what "executing" means.

Monday I wrote about Rust's memory-safety proof — an 11-year-old hole exposing the premise the proof rests on. Here is the mirror image: the most-deployed server language on the web, whose security model predates the modern threat model entirely, calling an emergency patch window while an EU agency briefs the offline switch. Two runtimes, two philosophies, same week — and both stories are the same story: the premise is part of the proof.

Run it yourself: the audit, the watch, the switch

The details of the vulnerability are withheld until the patch lands — so the receipts that matter right now are the ones on your side. Three pipelines:

1. The inventory — find every PHP on the machines you control:

# what's installed (Debian/Ubuntu and RHEL families)
dpkg -l | grep -E "php[0-9.]*-" | awk '{print $2, $3}'
rpm -qa | grep -E "^php" | sort

# what actually executes, and since when
php -v 2>/dev/null; php-fpm -v 2>/dev/null

# every PHP binary on disk, including the ones a panel installed years ago
sudo find / -name "php*" -type f -perm -111 2>/dev/null | grep -vE "/proc|/sys" | head -20

That last command is the one that finds the forgotten PHP 5.6 sitting in a panel directory that nobody has touched since 2019 — the exact asset CERT-EU's advisory exists for.

2. The exposure — what faces the internet right now:

# php-fpm sockets and pools
ss -tlnp | grep -E "php|9000"
# every vhost routing to PHP
grep -rE "php|fastcgi" /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/ 2>/dev/null | wc -l

3. The watch — until the patch lands, the exploit probes are your tripwire. You don't know the signature yet, so watch the volume and the weirdness:

# requests hitting PHP endpoints, last hour, with response codes
awk -v d="$(date -d '1 hour ago' '+%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M')" '$0 ~ d' /var/log/nginx/access.log \
  | grep -E "\.php" | awk '{print $1, $9}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

Spikes of POSTs to .php paths on sites that have no PHP forms, or 200s from paths that should 404 — that is your "currently not aware of active exploitation" turning into "aware."

4. The switch — when the patch drops at 14:00 GMT:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade "php*"
sudo systemctl restart php8.3-fpm   # your version
php -v                                # confirm the new release

And the offline switch CERT-EU is briefing — for assets you cannot patch in the window:

sudo systemctl stop php8.3-fpm
# serve a static maintenance page with no PHP in the path:
# nginx: return 503 with a maintenance root; the runtime is out of the request path entirely.

Stopping php-fpm removes the runtime from the request path — no PHP executing, no PHP vulnerability executing. It is the crudest control in this post and the only one CERT-EU explicitly endorsed for the unpatchable.

What you actually get

  • A deadline: 14:00 GMT today. The details land with the patch; the audit above is everything you can do before reading them.
  • A decision tree: can patch in the window → patch and verify the version. Can't patch → the offline switch, or take the asset off the internet edge. Don't know if you're exposed → the inventory commands exist for exactly that.
  • The honest limits: nothing in this post tells you whether you're vulnerable to these specific flaws — PHP publishes that when the patch lands. What the audit tells you is where every PHP lives, which is the prerequisite for patching in minutes instead of days.

And the premise note, because it's the same week: memory safety in the runtime is not an academic property. Eleven years of a proof on one side, an EU offline advisory on the other. The language your server runs is your attack surface's foundation — everything above it is scaffolding.

The patch drops at 14:00 GMT. The audit takes ten minutes. Do the audit first.

Sources: Reuters — EU agency warns websites may need to be taken offline as PHP prepares patches (Oct 21, 2026 — quoting CERT-EU, ACSC, GoDaddy, Huntress, PHP security team). The runtime-as-premise framing follows my Rust memory-safety post. Watch this post's dev.to comments — I'll update with the CVE details and fixed versions after the 14:00 GMT release.

articles.description: I recently bought the domain got-a.page and turned it into a free, community-run subdomain service....
articles.body_html:
I recently bought the domain got-a.page and turned it into a free, community-run subdomain service. Anyone can claim a name like yourname.got-a.page with one small JSON file and one pull request. No hosting bill, no registrar account, no ads, no tracking.

This guide walks through the whole thing: picking a name, choosing a mode, opening the PR, and what to expect after it merges.

What is got-a.page?

got-a.page gives you a free subdomain for your profile, product, project or community. Claims live in a public GitHub repo, one JSON file per page, and a maintainer merges them. There are two ways to use your name:

Instant mode - no website? We host the page for you.
Fill in your name, a tagline and your links, and a fast, accessible page is rendered at yourname.got-a.page. Light and dark mode included, in one of six themes: sunrise, lagoon, forest, plum, slate, ember. Person and product pages are supported today.

{
  "mode": "instant",
  "owner": { "github": "yourusername" },
  "page": {
    "type": "person",
    "title": "Your Name",
    "tagline": "What you're about, in one line",
    "avatar": "https://github.com/yourusername.png",
    "theme": "sunrise",
    "links": [{ "label": "GitHub", "url": "https://github.com/yourusername" }],
    "sections": [{ "heading": "About", "text": "A few sentences about you." }]
  }
}

Point mode - already hosting somewhere?
Point your name at GitHub Pages, Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, or anywhere that gives you a hostname or IP. CNAME, A, AAAA and TXT records are supported. One DNS rule to know: a CNAME can't be combined with other record types on the same name.

{
  "mode": "point",
  "owner": { "github": "yourusername" },
  "purpose": "My portfolio",
  "records": { "CNAME": "yourusername.github.io" }
}

You can switch modes later by editing your file with a new PR. And yes, it's really free: the domain is paid for years ahead and everything else runs on free tiers.

Before you start

  • A GitHub account. Claims are tied to it: owner.github must match the PR author, and only you (or a maintainer) can edit or remove your page later.
  • A name that's 2-40 characters of lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens.
  • Up to 2 pages per GitHub account while we're young.
  • Everything in the repo is public, forever. Don't put private data in your file.

Step 1: Open the guided claim form

Go to got-a.page/claim. The form writes the JSON for you, so you never touch raw JSON. There's a name checker on the homepage if you want to see whether your name is free first.

Step 2: Answer a few questions

Enter your page name, pick instant or point mode, and fill in the fields. Instant mode asks for your title, tagline, theme and links. Point mode asks for the DNS target your host recommends.

Step 3: Propose it on GitHub

The button at the end opens the claim repo on GitHub with your file prefilled. GitHub will ask you to fork (one click), then you choose "Propose changes" and open the pull request.

Automated validation checks review your file. Follow the check results on your PR - fork PRs don't get automatic bot comments, so the checks are where the feedback lives. A maintainer merges when it looks good.

Never made a pull request before? The repo's contributing guide walks you through every click. It's a kind place for your first one.

Step 4 (point mode only): connect your host before merge

This is the step people miss. A merged claim creates DNS records, but it does not add the domain to your hosting account. Add yourname.got-a.page on your host before the claim is merged:

  • GitHub Pages: your website repo > Settings > Pages > Custom domain, enter yourname.got-a.page, Save. Use "records": { "CNAME": "yourusername.github.io" } in your claim.
  • Vercel: your project > Settings > Domains > Add Domain. Copy the project-specific CNAME target Vercel gives you into your claim.
  • Netlify: Domain management > Add a domain you already own. Keep external DNS and copy the recommended target (usually your-site.netlify.app).
  • Cloudflare Pages: your Pages project > Custom domains > Set up a domain. Use your your-site.pages.dev target.

The docs at got-a.page/docs have the full per-host walkthrough.

What to expect after your PR merges

Instant mode: your page goes live within a few minutes. Until the index republishes, your address may still show the "unclaimed" page - that's normal, give it a few minutes and hard-refresh.

Point mode: DNS publishes first, then your host verifies the domain and issues its HTTPS certificate. Browsers will show a privacy or certificate error for your address during that window. That's expected - minutes to hours, occasionally longer. GitHub documents up to 24 hours for Enforce HTTPS to become available; turn it on once you can.

One HTTPS note: .page is on the HSTS preload list, so browsers force HTTPS on every got-a.page address. Instant pages are always secure (handled for you), and point-mode targets must serve valid HTTPS or browsers will refuse to load them. All the hosts above do that automatically once the custom domain is added.

"Is it broken?" - troubleshooting

What you see What's going on
Certificate/privacy error right after merge (point mode) Normal. Your host's certificate isn't ready yet. Wait, then enable Enforce HTTPS when offered.
Your old yourname.github.io shows the same error Expected. GitHub Pages redirects the old address to your custom domain as soon as you save it, so both show the error during the wait and both recover together.
Your address still says "unclaimed" (instant mode) The index hasn't republished yet. A few minutes, then hard-refresh.
Page loads but looks unstyled Your site is loading CSS/JS from the old address or over http://. Use relative asset URLs or update your static site generator's base URL setting.
Still stuck after a day Open an issue in the claim repo with your page name and what you see. Real humans read them.

The rules, short version

  • Claim with your own GitHub account.
  • Your page is public. Everything in the repo is public.
  • No phishing, scams, malware, impersonation, illegal or adult content.
  • Some names are reserved (service addresses, brand names, and words that would make the place less welcoming).
  • See abuse? Email abuse@got-a.page.

Extras

Badges: once your page is live, grab an "I got a page" or "Launched on got-a.page" badge from got-a.page/badges - HTML and Markdown snippets, ready to paste into your README.

What's coming later: more page types (project, community and event templates), a Wall of Pages gallery, and email on your subdomain. None of that is live yet - I'm adding it in later phases, and everything above is what works today.

Wrap up

  1. Check your name on got-a.page
  2. Claim it at got-a.page/claim
  3. Open the PR, follow the checks, done

Claim repo: github.com/got-a-page/claim - MIT licensed, and issues and first PRs are welcome. If you claim a page, drop your new address in the comments. I'd love to see what you make of it.

got-a.page is free and runs on my own time, so if it saved you a domain bill, consider sponsoring me to keep it going
