articles.title: Experiments in Software Factories #1: Production app in 40 minutes
articles.description: pastmonday.com is a real SaaS: auth, billing, uploads, and AI chat. A software factory of four Claude Code skills built it in about 40 minutes, and every backend service on the bill is Neon, including the brand new Object Storage and AI Gateway.
articles.body_html:
pastmonday.com is live. It has auth, a weekly calendar, tiered billing with Stripe, referral credits, file uploads, and an AI chat that knows your calendar. A small but complete SaaS, the kind of thing that used to be a three-month project.

Two things about it are unusual, and they're the reason for this post.

First: I didn't hand-write it. A software factory did.. four reusable Claude Code skills that turn a one-page brief into a shipped product, stage by stage. I talked about this on YouTube recently, and the skills themselves are public on GitHub.

Second: look at the vendor list. Postgres is Neon. Auth is Neon. The data API is Neon. Object storage is Neon. The LLM calls go through Neon. Stripe handles money and my own cluster serves the containers, and that's the entire list. The backend is one vendor, and until a few weeks ago that sentence was impossible to say, because half of these services didn't exist.

Neon announced they're building the full backend: Postgres, Auth, and the Data API are GA, and Object Storage, Functions, and an AI Gateway just entered private preview. I got early access, pointed the factory at all of it, and this post is the build report.

Note: this post is a transcription of my video on software factories, passed through AI and edited for reading. If you'd rather watch than read, here it is:

▶ Watch: Software Factories are SCARY but possible (and easy to do)

TL;DR

  • A software factory, four reusable Claude Code skills reading one PROJECT.md brief, shipped pastmonday.com from empty repo to production in about 40 minutes.
  • The entire backend is Neon: Postgres, Auth, and Data API (GA), plus Object Storage and AI Gateway (private preview, early access).
  • Money and limits are server-authoritative: atomic single-statement quota consumes, idempotent Stripe webhooks, AI budgets checked before every call.
  • The AI Gateway's official SDK provider wasn't installable yet, so the agent verified the OpenAI-compatible endpoint live and shipped anyway.. the API-first thesis from my last Neon post, proven again.
  • Neon now ships agent skills for their new services. The factory and the platform are converging.

Resources

  • The video: Software Factories are SCARY but possible
  • The factory skills on GitHub
  • pastmonday.com, the shipped product
  • Neon: we're building backends
  • My series: How To Build Any Web Application

The software factory

The core idea is one separation: the skill is the HOW, the brief is the WHAT.

Everything project-specific lives in a single PROJECT.md in the repo: name, one-liner, the plans table, the palette and fonts, the entities, which services are enabled. Everything reusable lives in the skills. When I want a different product, I write a different brief. The factory doesn't change.

There are four stages, each a separate skill, each reading that same brief:

  1. Foundation (set-project-structure) builds the skeleton: Next.js with the directory contracts, the Drizzle schema, env keys with comments on where to get each value, design tokens, and placeholder clients for every enabled service. It deliberately builds less: seams, not features.
  2. Landing (set-landing-page) is the taste stage. It studies the brief's reference sites, writes real copy before layout, and works against an explicit banned-patterns list: no gradient hero, no "Supercharge your workflow", no fake testimonials.
  3. Backend (set-app-backend) is the correctness stage. Money and limits. Every quota, credit, token budget, and dollar is enforced on the server, atomically, idempotently. More on this below, because this is where Neon's new services plug in.
  4. Dashboard (set-dashboard) builds the app people live in: the calendar, the modals, the streaming AI chat, consuming only the contracts stage 3 exposed.

Each stage stops at an approval gate before building, verifies current package versions instead of trusting its training data, and must leave the repo shippable when it ends. No half-built sections, no "we'll polish later".

Click through the stages here.. this is the actual pipeline that built pastmonday:

▶ The software factory pipeline (interactive), an interactive widget, runs on the original post.

I've written the first three stages up in detail before, if you want the deep dives: the concept, the brief, and the landing page.

What matters for this post: a factory like this is only as good as the surfaces it builds on. Stage 3 is where the factory has to wire auth, storage, data access, and LLM calls, and that's usually where you accumulate vendors. One for identity, one for buckets, one for model routing, plus the database. Four dashboards, four bills, four sets of credentials to leak.

This time, all four seams landed on the same platform.

One backend

Here's what pastmonday actually runs on, and the state of each piece:

Service Role in pastmonday Status
Postgres entries, profiles, billing, referrals, asset metadata GA
Neon Auth signup, login, sessions, the identity table GA
Data API PostgREST-style HTTP reads GA
Object Storage user file uploads, S3-compatible private preview
AI Gateway all LLM calls, metered per request private preview

A few receipts from the codebase, because "it works" is cheap to say.

Auth ships its own schema. Identity lives in neon_auth.user, and the factory's rule is: never mirror it. App tables hold foreign keys straight into it, so there's no sync job, no webhook that copies users around, no second source of truth:

// Neon Auth's identity schema, referenced, never mirrored
export const neonAuth = pgSchema("neon_auth");
export const authUser = neonAuth.table("user", { id: text("id").primaryKey() });

// profiles FK straight into it
userId: text("user_id").notNull()
  .references(() => authUser.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),

Storage speaks S3, so there's no proprietary SDK to learn. The client is the plain AWS SDK, and it auto-reads the endpoint from AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3. Uploads are presigned PUTs with keys scoped per user, and since a presigned PUT can't enforce a size limit, the confirm route does a HeadObject and deletes anything oversized. The interesting part: Neon's storage branches with your database. Every branch gets its own isolated storage state. Your files and your rows stop drifting apart across environments.

AI Gateway is one API for models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and others, with per-request logging and rate limits, running on the same gateway infrastructure Databricks says handles 125 trillion tokens a month. For the app it means one token in the environment instead of a drawer full of provider keys, and the model is a config value:

const provider = createOpenAICompatible({
  name: "neon-ai-gateway",
  baseURL: `${NEON_AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL}/ai-gateway/mlflow/v1`,
  apiKey: process.env.NEON_AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN,
});
export const chatModel = provider(process.env.NEON_AI_GATEWAY_MODEL);

Poke around the real architecture here, every box is clickable:

▶ pastmonday's backend, all Neon (interactive), an interactive widget, runs on the original post.

Building on features that shipped last week

In the last Neon post I made one argument: Neon is API-first, so an agent can reach a primitive the moment it exists, before anyone builds it a button. I proved it by building a feature Neon hadn't shipped yet.

This build pushed that idea further than I expected, twice.

First, the AI Gateway is so new that its official AI SDK provider package wasn't even installable yet when the factory ran stage 3. A human would have stopped there. The agent didn't: it probed the gateway, found the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at /ai-gateway/mlflow/v1, verified it live with a real request, and wired the app through the AI SDK's generic OpenAI-compatible provider instead. The code carries a comment saying "swap to the official provider once it installs". That's what API-first buys you: the endpoint existed, so the missing package didn't matter.

Second, the convergence I didn't see coming: a week after I published my factory skills, Neon shipped agent skills of their own.. instruction files that teach coding agents how to integrate Functions, Storage, and the AI Gateway, installable with one command:

npx skills add neondatabase/agent-skills

Read that again from where I'm standing. I write skills that teach an agent how to build products. Neon now writes skills that teach the same agent how to consume their platform. The factory and the platform are meeting in the middle, and neither side needed the other's permission. This is what it looks like when a vendor treats agents as the primary developer.

The part that has to be exactly right

A factory that ships beautiful broken apps is a liability, so stage 3 is paranoid by design. pastmonday charges money and sells limits: Free gets 1 entry and a 5,000-token AI budget, Pro gets 10 entries and 20,000 tokens a cycle, Max is unlimited. Limits only mean something if they can't be raced.

One constraint made this sharper than usual: the factory wired Drizzle through Neon's HTTP driver, which doesn't do interactive transactions. No BEGIN, hold the lock, decide, COMMIT. So every money-critical operation had to become a single atomic statement. This is the actual entry creation, quota check and insert in one round trip:

WITH consumed AS (
  UPDATE billing
     SET used_this_cycle = CASE WHEN used_this_cycle < monthly_quota
                                THEN used_this_cycle + 1 ELSE used_this_cycle END,
         extra_credits   = CASE WHEN used_this_cycle >= monthly_quota AND extra_credits > 0
                                THEN extra_credits - 1 ELSE extra_credits END
   WHERE profile_id = ${profileId}
     AND (used_this_cycle < monthly_quota OR extra_credits > 0)
  RETURNING id
)
INSERT INTO calendar_entries (user_id, title, ...)
SELECT ${userId}, ${title}, ...
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM consumed)

Quota first, then credits, else nothing gets inserted and the caller gets a 402. Two concurrent requests can't both take the last unit, not because the code is careful, but because the statement can't be split.

The same paranoia runs through the rest: the AI budget is checked server-side before every gateway call and metered from real usage on finish, Stripe webhooks dedupe on event id in a processed_stripe_events ledger so a replayed event can't grant credits twice, and quota-exhausted returns a typed 402 the UI turns into an upgrade prompt instead of an error toast.

None of this is Neon-specific, but it's the standard the factory holds, and the new services slotted into it without a fight. That's the actual test of a backend platform: not the demo, the enforcement paths.

Where this goes: branches that fork the whole stack

My favorite Neon primitive has always been branching. I've built preview environments where every pull request gets its own database branch, created and destroyed by the agent through the API.

The new services extend that idea past the database. Storage state branches with your data today, and Neon manages Functions through the same CLI and API as everything else. The direction is obvious and they're saying it out loud: a branch should fork the backend, not just the schema.

For a software factory, that's the missing piece. Today my factory pipeline validates each stage against the production-shaped environment it builds. The version I want is: every factory run, every agent session, every experiment gets a full isolated copy of the backend.. rows, files, functions.. for the lifetime of a task, then vanishes. Database branching already proved this workflow for schema changes. Extending it to the whole backend turns "spin up a staging environment" from an afternoon of Terraform into a flag on a CLI call.

That's the same story as the spending-caps feature from my last post, which is still marked "coming soon" by the way, and I'm still holding them to it: the primitives ship first, through the API, and the people building on top get to run ahead of the roadmap.

Closing

The pitch for this stack isn't "Neon does everything". It's narrower and more honest: a full working SaaS.. identity, data, files, AI, money.. now fits in one brief, four skills, one backend vendor, and one Stripe account. pastmonday went from empty repo to production on my cluster in about 40 minutes, and most of that time I was making taste decisions at the approval gates, not doing integration work.

If you want to go deeper: the video covers the factory concept, the skills are on GitHub to steal, the series walks each stage, and pastmonday.com is the living proof.. go create an entry, that's a race-safe atomic quota consume you're clicking.

And if you're at Neon: ship the branch-forks-everything future. I have a factory waiting for it.

articles.title: 40 Bytes a Call, Just to Pass Four Ints
articles.description: A params array allocates a fresh array on every call. Switching the parameter to params ReadOnlySpan<int> dropped that to zero bytes and ran 2.5x faster, measured.
articles.body_html:
I was staring at an allocation profile for a hot code path. The helper does almost nothing: it stamps a few counters onto a log line a few thousand times a second. And yet there was a column of int[] allocations in the profile I couldn't place. Nothing in my code newed up an array. I grepped for new int[. Nothing. The arrays were real though, and they were adding up.

Turned out I'd been allocating them for years without typing the word new once. They were hiding behind params.

Where the array comes from

Here's the shape of the thing. You write a method that takes a variable number of values:

static long Sum(params int[] xs)
{
    long acc = 0;
    foreach (int x in xs) acc += x;
    return acc;
}

And you call it the obvious way:

Sum(a, b, c, d);

That call site is a lie, or at least it hides the truth. The compiler can't pass four loose ints into a method that wants an int[], so it quietly builds one: Sum(new int[] { a, b, c, d }). Every call. A fresh four-element array on the heap, used for a few nanoseconds, then thrown to the GC. Nobody wrote new, but it's there in the IL all the same.

For most code that's fine. You call it once, who cares. On a path that runs thousands of times a second, those little arrays become a steady drip into gen 0, and gen 0 collections aren't free.

The fix is one word

Since C# 13 you can declare the params parameter as a span instead:

static long Sum(params ReadOnlySpan<int> xs)
{
    long acc = 0;
    foreach (int x in xs) acc += x;
    return acc;
}

The body is identical. The call site Sum(a, b, c, d) is identical too. What changes is what the compiler emits to carry the arguments: instead of a heap array, it stack-allocates the buffer (an inline array under the hood) and hands the method a span over it. No heap, no array, nothing for the GC to clean up.

The nice part is you don't have to touch any callers. If both overloads existed, C# 13's overload resolution prefers the span one. So the move is: add the span version, delete the array version, recompile. Call sites don't notice.

I counted it

I didn't want to take the compiler's word for it, so I wrote the smallest thing that would show the gap. Two methods, same arithmetic, called five million times each with four int arguments. I read GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around each loop and took the best of seven rounds.

long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++)
    acc += body(i);           // calls Sum(i, i+1, i+2, i+3)
sw.Stop();
long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();

Here's what came back:

iterations per round : 5,000,000  (best of 7)
args per call        : 4 ints

params int[]          time     62.0 ms   allocated    200,000,000 bytes
params ReadOnlySpan    time     25.1 ms   allocated              0 bytes

bytes per call (array) : 40.0
bytes per call (span)  : 0.0
time ratio array/span  : 2.47x

Forty bytes a call. That's exactly a four-element int[] on 64-bit: object header plus the length plus sixteen bytes of actual ints. The span version: zero. Not "less." Zero bytes, and it ran about two and a half times faster in the same loop, mostly because it isn't touching the allocator at all.

This isn't a lab. It's a container with workstation GC, and I care about the ratio and the allocation count, not the absolute milliseconds, which move around depending on where it runs. But 40 bytes versus 0 doesn't move. That's a structural difference, not a timing fluke.

The catch, because there's always one

A span can't escape. That's the whole deal with ref struct, and it's exactly the constraint that lets the compiler keep the buffer on the stack. So the moment your method wants to do any of these, the span version won't compile, and that's correct. It's stopping you from keeping a pointer to a stack frame that's about to disappear:

  • store the arguments in a field for later
  • return them, or hand them to something that outlives the call
  • await across the point where you're still using them

If you need the values to stick around, you need a real array, and params T[] is the honest way to get one. Don't fight the compiler here. Reach for the span version on the leaf methods that consume their arguments right now and return, which, if you look, is most of them. Formatters, aggregators, little Combine/Max/Sum helpers, logging shims. That's where the drip was coming from in my case, and that's where it stopped.

My honest opinion: for any new internal helper that takes params of a value type and uses it immediately, the span version should be the default and the array version the thing you reach for when you actually need an array. It's the same code to write, the call sites are untouched, and you stop paying a tax you probably forgot you were paying.

I'd been paying it for years. Go look at your own hot paths for params T[] on methods that just read their arguments and return — I'd bet there's a quiet little column of arrays in there too.

The whole thing

Here's the complete program if you want to run it yourself. New console project on the .NET 10 SDK (dotnet new console), drop this in Program.cs, then dotnet run -c Release:

using System.Diagnostics;

static long SumArray(params int[] xs)
{
    long acc = 0;
    foreach (int x in xs) acc += x;
    return acc;
}

static long SumSpan(params ReadOnlySpan<int> xs)
{
    long acc = 0;
    foreach (int x in xs) acc += x;
    return acc;
}

const int Iterations = 5_000_000;
const int Rounds = 7;
long sink = 0;

static (double ms, long bytes) Measure(int iterations, Func<int, long> body)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) body(i);   // warm up the JIT
    GC.Collect();
    GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
    GC.Collect();

    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    long acc = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) acc += body(i);
    sw.Stop();
    long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    return (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, after - before);
}

double bestArray = double.MaxValue, bestSpan = double.MaxValue;
long bytesArray = 0, bytesSpan = 0;

for (int r = 0; r < Rounds; r++)
{
    var a = Measure(Iterations, i => { long v = SumArray(i, i + 1, i + 2, i + 3); sink += v; return v; });
    var s = Measure(Iterations, i => { long v = SumSpan(i, i + 1, i + 2, i + 3); sink += v; return v; });
    if (a.ms < bestArray) { bestArray = a.ms; bytesArray = a.bytes; }
    if (s.ms < bestSpan) { bestSpan = s.ms; bytesSpan = s.bytes; }
}

Console.WriteLine($"params int[]          time {bestArray,8:F1} ms   allocated {bytesArray,14:N0} bytes");
Console.WriteLine($"params ReadOnlySpan    time {bestSpan,8:F1} ms   allocated {bytesSpan,14:N0} bytes");
Console.WriteLine($"bytes per call (array) : {(double)bytesArray / Iterations:F1}");
Console.WriteLine($"time ratio array/span  : {bestArray / bestSpan:F2}x");

What's the sneakiest allocation you've found hiding behind syntax you thought was free? Drop it in the comments.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: Processes vs Threads, as the Linux Kernel Sees Them
articles.description: Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for...
articles.body_html:
Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product.

"What is the difference between a process and a thread?"

You have been asked this. You have probably asked it.

The standard answer goes: a process is heavy, a thread is light, and threads share memory.

That answer is true.

It is also the kind of true that you can recite for ten years without ever understanding what is going on underneath.

So let's skip the textbook and look at both from the seat where the decisions actually get made.

The kernel's seat.

Start with one long bar of RAM

Picture your machine's memory as a single long bar. Say 16 GB.

All of it belongs to the kernel. No program is allowed to touch it directly.

When you launch an app, the kernel creates a process to represent it, and carves out a slice of the bar as that process's private memory.

It writes down who owns which slice in a notebook, and it guards those boundaries.

Now watch it with real software.

You open a photo editor. The kernel makes a process for it, and the editor fills its slice with a 5 MB photo.

You also have Spotify open. That is a second process, with a second slice further down the bar.

The editor cannot read Spotify's memory. Spotify cannot read your photo.

If the editor reaches outside its slice, the kernel stops it on the spot.

And if Spotify crashes, your photo does not even flinch.

That wall is the entire reason one program cannot read or corrupt another's data.

A small confession about the bar

The bar is a teaching picture, and it is a little too tidy.

Real kernels do not hand out literal chunks of physical RAM. Every process gets its own virtual address space, and the CPU's memory management unit translates those addresses through page tables that the kernel controls.

Two processes can both use "address 0x1000" and land on completely different physical memory.

Touch an address that is not mapped for you, and the hardware raises a fault, and the kernel typically answers with a SIGSEGV.

The kernel's own memory docs cover the concepts if you want the full tour.

The wall in the picture is a very real wall. It is just made of page tables instead of drywall.

Now the editor wants to be fast

Brightening a photo one pixel at a time on a single core is slow.

So the editor asks the kernel for help: "give me four threads".

Here is the part that matters.

The kernel does not hand each thread more RAM.

It creates four lightweight tasks and points all of them at the same slice the process already owns.

Then it schedules those four tasks onto four cores, and they run at the same moment.

Each thread takes a quarter of the photo and brightens its own region, reading and writing the pixels directly where they sit.

Nothing was copied.

When the last thread finishes, the whole image is already brighter.

Now imagine doing the same job with four processes instead.

Each one needs its own slice. So the photo gets copied into all four, which is four times the memory.

Then somebody has to collect the four finished pieces and stitch them back together, which means sending data between processes with pipes, sockets or shared memory.

That is the entire pitch for threads in one sentence: they skip the copy, and they skip the stitching.

A fairness note for processes

I have been a bit mean to processes, so let me correct the record.

Modern fork() does not actually copy the whole photo up front. On Linux it is implemented with copy-on-write pages.

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as parent
    participant K as kernel
    participant C as child

    P->>K: fork()
    K-->>C: new task, page tables copied, pages not copied
    Note over P,C: both see the same 5 MB, marked read-only
    C->>K: write to one pixel
    K->>K: page fault, copy just that one 4 KB page
    K-->>C: retry the write on the private copy
    Note over P,C: every untouched page is still shared

So the child starts almost for free, and only pays for pages it actually changes.

The picture above is the worst case, where every process rewrites everything. That is the case that happens when a job really does touch the whole photo.

The real difference is not "copy vs no copy" so much as "shared by default" vs "private by default".

And that, as we are about to see, is where all the trouble comes from.

The kernel's dirty secret: they are the same thing

Here is the sentence that rewired my head.

To the Linux kernel, a process and a thread are nearly the same object.

Both are just a task that the scheduler puts onto a CPU.

The scheduler does not schedule "processes". It schedules tasks. A four-thread process is four tasks that happen to be friends.

The only real difference is memory:

  • make a new task with a fresh slice, and you have a process
  • make a new task pointed at an existing slice, and you have a thread

On Linux that choice is one function: clone(), and one flag: CLONE_VM.

Do not take my word for it. Here is a tiny program that does the same write twice, once from a child process and once from a thread:

int brightness = 0;

void *worker(void *arg) { brightness = 100; return NULL; }

int main(void) {
    pid_t child = fork();
    if (child == 0) { brightness = 100; _exit(0); }   // a process writes
    waitpid(child, NULL, 0);
    printf("after a child PROCESS wrote 100: brightness = %d\n", brightness);

    pthread_t t;
    pthread_create(&t, NULL, worker, NULL);            // a thread writes
    pthread_join(t, NULL);
    printf("after a THREAD wrote 100:        brightness = %d\n", brightness);
}

I compiled it and ran it on Ubuntu 24.04:

after a child PROCESS wrote 100: brightness = 0
after a THREAD wrote 100:        brightness = 100

Same line of code in both. The process wrote into its own copy and the parent never saw it. The thread wrote into the copy.

Then I ran the same binary under strace -f -e trace=clone,clone3 to see what glibc really asked the kernel for (trimmed a little):

clone(child_stack=NULL, flags=CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID|CLONE_CHILD_SETTID|SIGCHLD)
clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|CLONE_SETTLS|...})

The first line is fork(). No CLONE_VM.

The second is pthread_create(). There it is, CLONE_VM, plus friends.

Those friends decide what else gets shared:

  • CLONE_FILES: the open file descriptors
  • CLONE_SIGHAND: the signal handlers
  • CLONE_THREAD: the new task joins the same thread group, which is why getpid() returns the same number for every thread and the kernel hands each one its own thread id instead

(In my run the main thread and the worker both reported the same pid, and the worker had its own tid. The man page for gettid covers the details.)

And what is private to each thread? Its own stack, its own registers, and its own thread-local storage. Everything else, the heap and the globals and the open files, is shared.

A fun side effect of all this: containers are the same trick. Namespaces are created with CLONE_NEW* flags on the same clone() call. Linux has one very flexible "make a task" function, and the whole zoo of processes, threads and containers is just different flag combinations.

Danger one: two threads, one pixel

Now for the bill.

The kernel let all four threads into the same memory. That is the whole point. It is also the whole problem.

If two threads write the same pixel at the same time, you get a race condition.

Here is how it goes wrong. Both threads add 10 to a pixel that holds 50:

Both read 50. Both compute 60. Both write 60.

You expected 70. You got 60.

There is no crash. There is no error. One brighten operation simply evaporated.

I wanted a real number instead of a hand-wavy one, so I ran four threads, each bumping one shared counter a million times:

for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
    unsafe++;                      // shared, no protection
    pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
    safe++;                        // shared, behind a mutex
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);
}

expected: 4000000
no lock:  3966879
mutex:    4000000

Over thirty thousand increments went missing, and the program exited happily. A second run lost a different amount.

That is what makes races miserable. They are not wrong in a consistent way. They are wrong in a different way every time, which is a spectacular property for a bug to have when you are trying to reproduce it.

The textbook fix is a lock. Only one thread at a time may touch the contended spot, and the rest wait their turn.

That works. It also costs you, because threads that wait are threads that are not working.

The better fix is to need no lock at all.

Look again at the photo example. Each thread was given its own quarter. Nobody writes anyone else's pixels, so nobody has to wait for anybody.

The best concurrency code is the kind where the threads rarely touch the same data. Partition first, lock only the seams.

Danger two: shared memory means shared fate

The second bill is nastier because it is not subtle.

All four threads live in one address space. So when one of them does something the kernel considers fatal, the kernel has no way of killing "just that thread".

A segmentation fault on any thread, and the default action for that signal is to terminate the whole process.

I did not want to just claim that, so I tried it. One thread ticks along. Another sleeps half a second, then writes through a null pointer:

steady thread: tick 1
steady thread: tick 2
steady thread: tick 3
Segmentation fault (core dumped)       # exit code 139

The steady thread had two more ticks to go. It never got them.

Three perfectly healthy threads, executed for the crime of sharing an address space with a guilty one.

The same logic applies to quieter failures. A buffer overflow in one thread can scribble over memory that another thread is using, and the crash shows up somewhere completely unrelated, an hour later.

Meanwhile Spotify, a separate process, is still playing. That wall from the first picture just paid for itself.

So which one do I pick?

You can see this trade-off baked into real software.

Chrome gives each site its own process, so one rogue tab cannot take the browser down with it. Isolation is worth the memory.

PostgreSQL uses a process per connection, so a crashing backend does not take the whole database with it. Isolation is worth the memory there too.

On the other side, anything that crunches one big shared dataset on many cores, like our photo brightener, wants threads, because copying and stitching would eat the speedup.

(And if you are in Python, the GIL means threads will not run your Python bytecode in parallel in the standard build, which is why so many people reach for processes there. That is a language story, not a kernel one.)

Here is the decision as a flowchart:

flowchart TD
    A[you need concurrency] --> B{must one failure<br/>stay contained?}
    B -->|yes: untrusted code,<br/>plugins, separate tenants| P[processes]
    B -->|no| C{do the workers need to<br/>share lots of data fast?}
    C -->|no| P2[processes,<br/>simpler and safer]
    C -->|yes| D{can you partition the data so<br/>threads rarely touch the same bytes?}
    D -->|yes| T[threads,<br/>almost no locks]
    D -->|no| T2[threads plus locks,<br/>and budget for the debugging]

    classDef decision fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef proc fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef thr fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a

    class B,C,D decision
    class A start
    class P,P2 proc
    class T,T2 thr

The 30 second interview answer

If somebody asks you the question tomorrow, here is the whole thing:

  1. The kernel gives every process its own private memory, and the wall between processes is why one app cannot corrupt another.
  2. A thread is a task the kernel points at memory that already exists, so threads share one address space and nothing gets copied.
  3. On Linux both are made by clone(). The difference is basically one flag, CLONE_VM.
  4. Sharing is the speed, and it is also the two dangers: races when threads touch the same data, and shared fate when one thread crashes.

"Threads are lightweight" was never wrong.

It just left out what you are paying with.

articles.title: Where Do Your Users' Passwords Actually Live? Self-Hosted vs Managed Keycloak
articles.description: Choosing between self-hosted and managed Keycloak affects more than where your identity service runs....
articles.body_html:
Choosing between self-hosted and managed Keycloak affects more than where your identity service runs. It determines who maintains the infrastructure, who handles security updates, and how much responsibility your team takes on when users need to authenticate.

When you add authentication to an application, it's easy to focus on the login screen. You choose between passwords and passkeys, connect an identity provider, and make sure users can access their accounts. But there's another question worth asking before your application goes live: where are your users' credentials stored, and who is responsible for protecting them?

Keycloak gives developers control over authentication and identity management. You can run it on infrastructure you manage, or use a managed Keycloak service that takes care of much of the underlying operation.

Both approaches can work well. The right choice depends on your security requirements, your team's infrastructure experience, your budget, and how much operational responsibility you're prepared to take on.

Let's look at what happens to user passwords in each setup, what changes when you choose a managed service, and how to decide which option makes sense for your application.

TL;DR

With self-hosted Keycloak, user credentials are stored in the Keycloak database that you configure and operate. Your team is responsible for securing that database, maintaining backups, applying updates, and protecting the infrastructure.

With Skycloak's managed Keycloak, you use the official upstream Keycloak platform without operating the underlying identity infrastructure yourself. Skycloak manages the infrastructure and provides automatic updates, while your team retains control over Keycloak configuration and remains responsible for integrating authentication securely into your application.

Here's the practical difference:

  • Self-hosted Keycloak: You control the deployment, database, network, updates, backups, and access policies. You also carry the operational burden of keeping everything secure and available.
  • Managed Keycloak with Skycloak: Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure while giving your team full Keycloak admin access. All plans support unlimited users, so pricing isn't tied to monthly active users.
  • Regions and portability: Skycloak offers deployment regions in the US, EU, Canada, and Australia, plus realm export options to help you plan a migration if you later choose to self-host.
  • Getting started: You can try Skycloak free for 21 days without providing a credit card.
  • Password security: Keycloak stores passwords as salted password hashes, not as readable plaintext passwords. Database access, configuration, backups, and administrative permissions still need protection.
  • Cost: Self-hosting can offer more infrastructure control, but server costs are only part of the total expense. Managed services add a service fee but can reduce the engineering time spent operating the identity platform.

The short answer: In a standard deployment, Keycloak handles authentication in both models. The main difference is who operates the identity infrastructure and how responsibilities are divided between your team and the provider. If you use an external user store, credential storage and verification may be handled partly or entirely by that system.

What Actually Happens to a Password in Keycloak?

Imagine someone creates an account in your application. They enter an email address, choose a password, and click Create account. Where does that password go?

In a typical Keycloak setup using its built-in user storage, Keycloak receives the password during account creation and stores a password hash in its configured database. A password hash is the output of a one-way password-hashing function. When the user signs in later, Keycloak verifies the submitted password against the stored hash. If an external user store handles authentication, credential storage and verification may follow a different process.

The database doesn't need to contain the original password in readable form. Keycloak uses a password-hashing algorithm and configuration designed to make guessing passwords computationally expensive. The exact algorithm and parameters depend on the Keycloak version and configuration.

Keycloak's default password-hashing algorithm depends on the version and deployment configuration. Keycloak 24 changed the default from pbkdf2-sha256 to pbkdf2-sha512. Starting with Keycloak 25, Argon2 became the default for non-FIPS deployments, while FIPS deployments use a compatible algorithm such as pbkdf2-sha512. Existing credentials may retain their previous hash until the user next signs in and Keycloak re-hashes the password under the current configuration.

To inspect or configure password policy settings, open the Keycloak Admin Console and navigate to Authentication → Policies → Password policy.

Review the policy configured for your realm before assuming it matches the defaults for a particular release.

Where Keycloak Stores Password Credentials

In a standard Keycloak deployment using its built-in user storage, password credentials are stored in the database configured for Keycloak. The CREDENTIAL table holds credential records associated with users, including password-related data and metadata.

Two fields help illustrate how that works:

  • SECRET_DATA: stores sensitive credential data, including password-hashing information.
  • CREDENTIAL_DATA: stores additional credential metadata, such as information about the credential type and its configuration.

These fields contain structured data, not a readable copy of the user's original password. The exact contents depend on the credential type and Keycloak version.

For example, a password credential record may contain data resembling the following. These are illustrative examples, not actual values from a live Keycloak database.

// SECRET_DATA — illustrative example
{
  "value": "[password hash omitted]",
  "salt": "[salt omitted]",
  "additionalParameters": {}
}

// CREDENTIAL_DATA — illustrative example
{
  "algorithm": "argon2",
  "hashIterations": "[configured value]",
  "additionalParameters": {}
}

The exact field names and structure can vary by Keycloak version and credential implementation.

Password Hashing Isn't the Whole Security Story

This distinction matters because password hashing and database security solve different problems. Hashing helps protect passwords if someone obtains a copy of the credential records, but it doesn't make a compromised identity server or database harmless. Attackers who gain administrative access may be able to alter accounts, change authentication settings, or access other sensitive information.

For example, your deployment still needs to protect:

  • Database access and administrative credentials.
  • Backups containing credential records and other sensitive data.
  • Keycloak configuration and privileged administrative accounts.
  • The infrastructure and network surrounding the identity service.

Where Is the Rest of the Identity Data Stored?

Your Keycloak deployment also holds information beyond password credentials, including user profiles, groups, roles, and configuration data. Depending on your setup, it may connect to external identity providers or use additional user-storage systems. The exact location of user data therefore depends on how the realm and user storage are configured.

For a standard deployment using Keycloak's built-in user storage, the password hashes are held in the configured database. If your environment uses an external user store, the credentials may be managed there instead.

This is the starting point for comparing self-hosted and managed Keycloak: the credential-handling model can remain the same, while the people responsible for the surrounding infrastructure change.

What Self-Hosted Keycloak Means

With self-hosted Keycloak, you deploy and operate the identity service on infrastructure under your team's control. That might be a virtual machine, a container platform, Kubernetes, or another supported environment.

You choose the deployment architecture, configure the database, manage network access, and decide how the service fits into your existing infrastructure. This gives you considerable flexibility, which can be valuable when an application has specific compliance requirements or needs to integrate with internal systems.

What Your Team Is Responsible For

The trade-off is that your team must take responsibility for operating the service reliably.

That includes:

  • Applying Keycloak security updates and testing upgrades.
  • Maintaining the database and testing backups and restores.
  • Monitoring availability and planning for service failures.
  • Protecting administrative accounts, TLS certificates, and network rules.
  • Reviewing configuration changes and tracking security advisories.

There's also the less visible work: testing recovery procedures and making sure they still work when you need them.

When Does Self-Hosting Make Sense?

Self-hosting can be a good fit when you need deep infrastructure control and have the people and processes to maintain it. It can also make sense when your organization already operates identity infrastructure and has established procedures for security, monitoring, and incident response.

But running Keycloak yourself doesn't automatically make your authentication more secure. The result depends on how well the service, database, network, and operational processes are configured and maintained.

What Changes With Managed Keycloak?

Managed Keycloak shifts much of the infrastructure work to a service provider. You still use Keycloak for identity management and authentication, but the provider operates the managed environment according to its service offering.

For a development team, that can mean less time spent maintaining servers, planning upgrades, monitoring infrastructure, and managing database operations. It can also make it easier to get an identity service running without first building an entire deployment and maintenance process.

What the Provider May Manage

The provider may manage:

  • Infrastructure provisioning and maintenance.
  • Database operations and backups.
  • Keycloak updates and upgrades.
  • Availability monitoring and infrastructure recovery.

What Still Belongs to Your Team?

However, managed Keycloak doesn't mean someone else automatically handles every aspect of authentication security.

Your team still needs to configure authentication flows, manage realm settings, assign appropriate roles, protect administrative access, and integrate the identity provider correctly with your application. You also need to decide how users are onboarded, how accounts are recovered, and what permissions they receive after signing in.

Data ownership and access deserve attention, too. Before choosing a provider, understand where your identity data is stored, who can access it, how backups are protected, and what happens when you decide to leave the service.

Managed Keycloak is useful when you want to use Keycloak's identity capabilities without taking on the full burden of operating the infrastructure.

Self-Hosted Keycloak vs Skycloak: A Practical Comparison

Both deployment models can use Keycloak's authentication features. The differences become clearer when you compare the responsibilities involved in running them.

Area Self-hosted Keycloak Skycloak
Infrastructure Your team provisions and operates it Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure
Database operations Your team configures, secures, and maintains the database Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure
Security updates Your team plans, tests, and applies updates Automatic updates
Backups and recovery Your team configures and tests backup and restore procedures Skycloak manages infrastructure, updates, backups, and scaling
Availability Your team designs and maintains availability Uptime commitments vary by plan; Business includes a 99.9% SLA, and Enterprise offers up to 99.99%
Configuration control Greater control over the deployment environment Full Keycloak admin access; Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure
Operational workload Higher infrastructure responsibility Reduced infrastructure maintenance for your team
Cost structure Infrastructure, engineering time, maintenance, and operational overhead Infrastructure-based pricing, unlimited users, and no fees tied to monthly active users

Self-hosted Keycloak gives your team direct control over the infrastructure and responsibility for operating it. Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure, while your team retains full Keycloak admin access and responsibility for securely integrating authentication into your application. All Skycloak plans support unlimited users, with pricing based on infrastructure rather than monthly active users.

Cost also deserves a realistic comparison. A self-hosted deployment might look cheaper when you compare only server expenses with a managed service's monthly fee. Once you include engineering time, monitoring, backups, upgrades, incident response, and availability requirements, the total cost can look different.

For a small team, reducing ongoing operational work may justify a managed service. For an organization with a mature platform engineering team and strict infrastructure requirements, self-hosting may be the better fit.

How Skycloak Makes Managed Keycloak Practical

Self-hosting Keycloak gives your team control, but that control comes with ongoing work: maintaining the deployment, applying updates, monitoring availability, and keeping the supporting infrastructure secure.

Skycloak provides managed hosting for upstream Keycloak. It manages the underlying infrastructure while giving your team full Keycloak admin access, so you can configure identity and authentication without operating the infrastructure yourself.

Keep Keycloak's Capabilities Without Running the Infrastructure

Skycloak runs upstream Keycloak and gives your team full Keycloak admin access. Its managed service includes the following benefits:

  • Less infrastructure maintenance: Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure, reducing the operational work your team handles.
  • Keycloak authentication features: Configure SSO, MFA, SAML, and OpenID Connect (OIDC).
  • Unlimited users: All plans support unlimited users, with no fees tied to monthly active users.
  • Regional deployment options: Paid plans offer supported deployment regions in the US, EU, Canada, and Australia.
  • Realm export: Export your realms to help plan a migration to a self-hosted Keycloak deployment.
  • Free trial: Try Skycloak for 21 days without a credit card.

For current pricing and plan details, visit the Skycloak pricing page.

What Does This Mean for Your Team?

Consider a small SaaS team building its product. The developers need authentication, user management, and secure access to application resources, but they may not have a dedicated platform team to maintain an identity deployment.

With self-hosted Keycloak, the team plans and maintains infrastructure provisioning, updates, backups, monitoring, and recovery alongside product development. With Skycloak, the provider manages the underlying infrastructure, while the team focuses on integrating Keycloak, configuring authentication flows, managing access, and securing application sessions.

This doesn't remove the need for sound identity and application security. Your team still needs to configure roles and permissions, protect administrative access, validate redirect URIs, and make sure authenticated users can access only the resources they're authorized to use.

The benefit is a clearer division of responsibilities: Skycloak operates the managed infrastructure, while your team focuses on using Keycloak securely within the application.

Is Skycloak Worth Considering?

Skycloak is worth considering if you want Keycloak's flexibility without operating the underlying infrastructure. All plans support unlimited users, and infrastructure-based pricing means your bill isn't tied to monthly active users. You can choose from supported deployment regions in the US, EU, Canada, and Australia, export realms when planning a migration, and try the service free for 21 days without a credit card.

Compare the available features and prices on the Skycloak pricing page.

Which Keycloak Deployment Should You Choose?

There's no universal winner. The right choice depends on your team's capabilities and the requirements of your application.

Choose self-hosted Keycloak if:

  • You need extensive control over the infrastructure, network, database, or deployment architecture.
  • Your organization already has people responsible for operating production services.
  • You have specific requirements that a managed provider cannot meet.
  • You're prepared to maintain upgrades, backups, monitoring, incident response, and disaster recovery.

Choose managed Keycloak with Skycloak if:

  • You want upstream Keycloak without operating the underlying identity infrastructure.
  • You want full Keycloak admin access while reducing infrastructure maintenance.
  • You need features such as SSO, MFA, OIDC, and SAML.
  • You want unlimited users without fees tied to monthly active users.
  • You need deployment options in the US, EU, Canada, or Australia.
  • Realm export and a 21-day free trial without a credit card fit your evaluation and migration plans.

For an early-stage SaaS product, Skycloak can provide a way to use Keycloak without building and maintaining the supporting infrastructure from scratch. Teams with established platform engineering capabilities or requirements that call for direct infrastructure control may prefer self-hosting. Evaluate both options against your security needs, engineering capacity, expected costs, and long-term plans.

Before committing, ask a few concrete questions: Can you configure the authentication flows you need? Can you export or migrate your identity data? What backup and recovery guarantees exist? Who applies security updates, and how are changes communicated? What happens if the provider experiences an outage?

Those answers will tell you more than the label managed or self-hosted alone.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where does Keycloak store user passwords?

→ In a standard Keycloak deployment using its built-in user storage, password credentials are stored as password hashes in the configured database. Keycloak does not need to store the original passwords in readable plaintext. If the deployment uses an external user store, credential storage may be handled by that system.

What is Skycloak, and how does it differ from self-hosted Keycloak?

→ Skycloak is a managed Keycloak service that runs the upstream Keycloak platform and manages the underlying infrastructure. With self-hosted Keycloak, your team operates the deployment and supporting services. With Skycloak, infrastructure responsibilities covered by the service move to the provider, while your team continues to manage application integration and identity configuration.

Can I use passkeys with self-hosted and managed Keycloak?

→ Yes. Keycloak supports WebAuthn-based authentication, including passwordless passkey flows, when configured appropriately. The exact setup depends on your Keycloak version, authentication flow, and environment. With a managed service, confirm that the provider supports the configuration and administrative access your application needs.

Who manages security when using Skycloak?

→ Security responsibilities are shared. Skycloak manages the underlying infrastructure, while your team uses its full Keycloak admin access to configure authentication, protect administrative accounts, assign appropriate permissions, and integrate Keycloak securely into the application. Your team should still verify any specific uptime, backup, and recovery commitments it requires.

Is self-hosted Keycloak cheaper than managed Keycloak?

→ It can be, but server costs alone don't show the full picture. Self-hosting also requires engineering time for updates, monitoring, backups, troubleshooting, and incident response. Managed Keycloak introduces service fees but may reduce those operational costs. Compare the total cost of ownership for your expected workload and team capacity.

Final Thoughts

Self-hosting gives you direct responsibility for the deployment, database, updates, and availability. Skycloak lets you keep using upstream Keycloak with full Keycloak admin access while the provider manages the underlying infrastructure.

All plans support unlimited users, and the service offers deployment regions in the US, EU, Canada, and Australia. You can try Skycloak for free for 21 days without a credit card.

Choose the setup that protects your users' identities and gives your team a clear, sustainable way to manage authentication as your product grows.
