articles.title: A liquid glass tab bar: the magnifying lens is a scaled copy of the bar
articles.description: How the lens in a liquid glass tab bar magnifies the icon under it without SVG filters, and how a spring's velocity stretches it like a drop. Plain HTML/CSS/JS demo, plus the Framer Motion version.
articles.body_html:
Apple's liquid glass tab bars have a lens that sits on the selected tab and magnifies the icon under it. When you switch tabs it moves like a drop of water: it stretches on the way, then settles.

Most web versions of this effect use an SVG displacement filter inside backdrop-filter. That only renders in Chromium browsers; Safari and Firefox skip it. I built one for a music-app demo and wanted it to look the same in every browser, so the lens uses no filter at all. It's a small window onto a second copy of the bar, scaled up 1.42 times.

This post covers three pieces:

  1. The glass bar (plain backdrop-filter).
  2. The lens: a clipped, scaled copy, and the one line of math that keeps it lined up.
  3. The drop: a spring whose speed sets the lens width.

There's a single-file demo at the end you can paste into CodePen. If you build with Cursor or Claude Code, it also works as a reference file to hand to your agent: it's short, and every number in it is explained here.

1. The glass bar

The bar itself is ordinary frosted glass. Blur plus saturation does most of the work. The inset shadows draw a light top edge and a faint 1px rim so the bar reads as a solid object on any background.

This is the CSS from the shipped component (tabbar-liquid.css):

.glassbar {
  position: absolute;
  border-radius: 32px;
  background: var(--glass);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
  backdrop-filter: blur(16px) saturate(1.9);
  box-shadow:
    inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.22),
    inset 0 0 0 1px var(--glass-line),
    0 18px 40px rgba(0,0,0,.45);
}

saturate(1.9) matters more than it looks. Blur alone washes colours out to grey. Saturation brings back the colour of whatever scrolls underneath, which is what makes it read as glass and not as a grey panel.

Keep the -webkit- prefix. Safari still wants it.

2. The lens is a copy, not a filter

Real magnification would need a displacement filter on whatever sits behind the lens. You can fake the part people actually notice, the icon under the lens getting bigger, with plain transforms:

  • Render the tabs a second time inside the lens element.
  • Give the lens overflow: hidden so you only see the part under it.
  • Scale the copy by M (1.42 here) around the lens centre.

The markup is a lens with an inner layer that holds the copy:

<div class="lens" aria-hidden="true">
  <div class="lensIn"><!-- the same tabs again, not focusable --></div>
</div>

The copy must stay out of the accessibility tree and out of the tab order, or a screen reader reads every tab twice. In the React component the copy is rendered with live={false}, which does exactly that:

const inert = live ? {} : { tabIndex: -1, 'aria-hidden': true as const };

The one line of math

.lensIn has transform-origin: 0 0 and fills the same box as the real bar. The lens has width w, height h, and centre (x, y) in bar coordinates, so its top-left corner is (lx, ly) = (x - w/2, y - h/2).

You want the point under the lens centre to stay where it is, with everything around it pushed outwards by M. Here's the render code from the shipped engine.ts:

const Ls = S.lens, lx = Ls.x - Ls.w / 2, ly = Ls.y - Ls.h / 2, M = 1.42;
lens.style.transform = `translate(${lx.toFixed(1)}px,${ly.toFixed(1)}px) scale(${Ls.sx.toFixed(4)},${Ls.sy.toFixed(4)})`;
lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${(-lx + Ls.x - M * Ls.x).toFixed(2)}px,${(-ly + Ls.y - M * Ls.y).toFixed(2)}px) scale(${M})`;

Why it works: a point p of the copy lands at M·p + t inside the lens, and the lens sits at lx. On screen that is lx + M·p + (-lx + x - M·x), which simplifies to x + M·(p - x). At p = x you get x, so the centre stays put and everything else spreads out from it by M. It's the textbook "scale around a point" transform, with the lens offset cancelled out.

Since the copy is real DOM, you can style it apart from the bar. Trimmed from the shipped CSS (the comments are mine):

.lens {
  position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; overflow: hidden; pointer-events: none;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,.07);
  backdrop-filter: blur(3px) saturate(2) brightness(1.18);
  box-shadow:
    inset 0 2px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.75),     /* bright top rim */
    inset 0 -2px 0 rgba(198,244,50,.55),     /* lime bottom rim */
    inset 0 -12px 20px rgba(139,108,255,.4),
    inset 5px 0 9px rgba(255,90,170,.35),    /* pink left edge */
    inset -5px 0 9px rgba(90,220,255,.35),   /* cyan right edge */
    0 0 0 1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.4),
    0 12px 28px rgba(0,0,0,.5),
    0 0 34px rgba(198,244,50,.42);
}
.lensIn { position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; transform-origin: 0 0; }
.lensIn .tab { color: var(--volt); }        /* the magnified icon turns lime */
.lensIn .tab i { opacity: 0 !important; }   /* hide the label inside the lens */
.lensIn .tab svg { translate: 0 8px; }      /* and drop the icon into the middle */
.lensIn .dockc {
  filter: drop-shadow(1.6px 0 0 rgba(255,70,150,.6))
          drop-shadow(-1.6px 0 0 rgba(70,210,255,.6));
}

Two details from that block:

  • The pink and cyan inset shadows on the left and right edges, plus two 1.6px drop-shadows on the copy, fake the colour fringing you see where real glass bends light. They're cheap and they sell the effect more than anything else in the file.
  • The label is hidden inside the lens and the icon moves down 8px. A magnified label gets cut off by the lens edge and looks like a bug. A centred icon looks deliberate.

The cost of this approach is that the content renders twice. For five icons that's nothing. The same component reuses the trick for a bigger orb that lifts out of the bar: the orb's copy holds the whole screen, scaled with the same formula.

3. The drop: speed sets the width

A lens that slides at a fixed width looks like a highlight pill. It reads as liquid once it stretches while it moves and goes back to round when it stops.

In the React version the lens x-position is a Framer Motion spring, and useVelocity reads how fast that spring is moving:

// live mode: the lens rides a spring, and its speed stretches the drop
const x = useSpring(tabX(0), { stiffness: 380, damping: 26 });
const stretch = useVelocity(x);

Every frame, the speed (px/s) maps to the lens size:

const v = Math.abs(stretch.get());
S.lens = {
  x: lx, y: g.cy,
  w: mix(66 + Math.min(92, v / 9), 56, c),
  h: mix(52 - Math.min(10, v / 90), 56, c),
  /* ... */
};

Leave out mix(..., c) for now. That's the compact state, when the bar shrinks on scroll. What's left:

  • At rest the lens is 66 × 52.
  • It gets 1px wider for every 9 px/s of speed, up to 92px more.
  • It gets thinner by up to 10px, so a fast move reads as a long, thin drop.
  • The clamps stop a very fast flick from stretching it across the whole bar.

The spring's overshoot does the rest. With stiffness 380 and damping 26 the spring is underdamped (damping ratio about 0.67), so it passes the target a little and comes back. The width follows the speed, so you get a wobble on landing without writing one keyframe.

Switching tabs is one line: x.set(tabX(i)).

Keyboard and screen readers

The real tabs are a tablist. Each tab gets role="tab" and aria-selected, and left/right arrows move between them:

if (e.key !== 'ArrowRight' && e.key !== 'ArrowLeft') return;
e.preventDefault(); i = (i + (e.key === 'ArrowRight' ? 1 : 4)) % 5;
screen.current?.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[data-dock] [data-tab]')[i]?.focus();

(+ 4 is - 1 modulo 5, so left arrow from the first tab wraps to the last.)

The lens, the copy and the rings are all aria-hidden. Only the real tabs are announced.

The single-file version

No Framer Motion here. The spring is about ten lines of Hooke's law with damping, using the same stiffness and damping as the React version. Paste it into CodePen's HTML panel or save it as a .html file and open it:

<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">

<title>Liquid glass tab bar: magnifying lens demo</title>
<!-- MIT licence. Teaching version of the lens from qodesign's Liquid Glass Tab Bar (qodesign.dev). -->
<style>

    <div class="bar"></div>
    <div class="tabs" role="tablist" aria-label="Sections" id="tabs"></div>
    <div class="lens" id="lens" aria-hidden="true"><div class="lensIn" id="lensIn"></div></div>

</div>
<script>

  ['Home',    '<path d="M3 11l9-7 9 7v9a1 1 0 0 1-1 1h-5v-6H9v6H4a1 1 0 0 1-1-1z"/>'],
  ['Explore', '<circle cx="12" cy="12" r="9"/><path d="M15.5 8.5l-2 5-5 2 2-5z"/>'],
  ['Library', '<path d="M4 4v16M9 4v16M14 4l6 16"/>'],
  ['Inbox',   '<path d="M4 13l2-8h12l2 8v6H4z"/><path d="M4 13h5l1 2h4l1-2h5"/>'],
  ['Profile', '<circle cx="12" cy="8" r="4"/><path d="M4 21c1.5-4 4.5-6 8-6s6.5 2 8 6"/>'],

const tabHTML = (live) => TABS.map(([label, icon], i) =>
  `<button class="tab" type="button" ${live ? `role="tab" aria-selected="${i === 0}" tabindex="${i ? -1 : 0}"` : 'tabindex="-1"'}>

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const dock = document.querySelector('.dock'), tabsEl = $('tabs'), lens = $('lens'), lensIn = $('lensIn');
tabsEl.innerHTML = tabHTML(true);
lensIn.innerHTML = `<div class="tabs">${tabHTML(false)}</div>`;   // the copy the lens magnifies
const tabs = [...tabsEl.children];
const M = 1.42;                                                     // magnification
const reduce = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');

// a tiny spring: same feel as Framer Motion's useSpring({ stiffness: 380, damping: 26 })
const spring = { x: 0, v: 0, target: 0, k: 380, c: 26 };
const centerOf = (i) => tabs[i].offsetLeft + tabs[i].offsetWidth / 2;
let active = 0;

function select(i, focus) {
  active = (i + tabs.length) % tabs.length;
  tabs.forEach((t, j) => { t.setAttribute('aria-selected', j === active); t.tabIndex = j === active ? 0 : -1; });
  if (focus) tabs[active].focus();
  spring.target = centerOf(active);
  if (reduce.matches) { spring.x = spring.target; spring.v = 0; }
}

function paint() {
  const W = dock.clientWidth, H = dock.clientHeight;
  lensIn.style.width = W + 'px'; lensIn.style.height = H + 'px';
  const speed = Math.abs(spring.v);                        // px per second
  const w = 66 + Math.min(92, speed / 9);                  // faster = longer drop
  const h = 52 - Math.min(10, speed / 90);                 // ...and a little thinner
  const x = Math.max(w / 2, Math.min(W - w / 2, spring.x));      // keep the drop inside the bar
  const y = H / 2, lx = x - w / 2, ly = y - h / 2;
  lens.style.width = w + 'px'; lens.style.height = h + 'px';
  lens.style.borderRadius = Math.min(w, h) / 2 + 'px';
  lens.style.transform = `translate(${lx}px, ${ly}px)`;
  // keep the point under the lens centre still, and scale everything around it
  lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${-lx + x - M * x}px, ${-ly + y - M * y}px) scale(${M})`;

let last = performance.now();
function frame(now) {
  const dt = Math.min(0.032, (now - last) / 1000); last = now;
  const a = -spring.k * (spring.x - spring.target) - spring.c * spring.v;   // Hooke + damping, mass 1
  spring.v += a * dt; spring.x += spring.v * dt;
  paint();
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}

// tap, drag across the bar, or use the arrow keys
const nearest = (clientX) => {
  const r = dock.getBoundingClientRect(), px = clientX - r.left;
  return tabs.reduce((best, t, i) => Math.abs(centerOf(i) - px) < Math.abs(centerOf(best) - px) ? i : best, 0);
};
tabsEl.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => { tabsEl.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); select(nearest(e.clientX)); });
tabsEl.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => { if (e.buttons) select(nearest(e.clientX)); });
tabsEl.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'ArrowRight') { e.preventDefault(); select(active + 1, true); }
  if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft')  { e.preventDefault(); select(active - 1, true); }
});
addEventListener('resize', () => { spring.target = spring.x = centerOf(active); });

spring.x = spring.target = centerOf(0);
requestAnimationFrame(frame);
</script>
</body>
</html>

The parts worth reading in the demo:

// a tiny spring: same feel as Framer Motion's useSpring({ stiffness: 380, damping: 26 })
const a = -spring.k * (spring.x - spring.target) - spring.c * spring.v;
spring.v += a * dt; spring.x += spring.v * dt;

const speed = Math.abs(spring.v);              // px per second
const w = 66 + Math.min(92, speed / 9);        // faster = longer drop
const h = 52 - Math.min(10, speed / 90);       // ...and a little thinner
const x = Math.max(w / 2, Math.min(W - w / 2, spring.x));   // keep the drop inside the bar
lensIn.style.transform = `translate(${-lx + x - M * x}px, ${-ly + y - M * y}px) scale(${M})`;

The demo adds three things the shipped component doesn't have:

  • Drag along the bar and the lens follows your finger to the nearest tab, stretching over every tab it passes.
  • It clamps the drop inside the bar, because a 158px drop on the last tab hangs off the edge.
  • With prefers-reduced-motion: reduce it jumps straight to the new tab, with no stretch and no wobble. Do that in anything you ship. A drop that stretches across the screen is exactly the kind of motion that setting is for.

Easy ways to get it wrong

  • Scaling the copy around its own centre. The magnified icon drifts sideways as the lens moves. Use transform-origin: 0 0 and put the whole offset in the translate.
  • A CSS transition on the lens width. The width then lags behind the position. Set width, height and transform in the same frame, all read from the spring.
  • A focusable copy. Keyboard users tab through ten tabs instead of five. Mark the copy aria-hidden and give every button in it tabindex="-1".
  • Labels inside the lens. They get cut by the lens edge. Hide them in the copy.

About me, and the links. I'm Teodor, and I make animated UI components at qodesign. The tab bar in this post is one of them, so this is partly a post about my own product. The demo above is MIT: copy it, change it, ship it. The full component adds the orb that turns into a full-screen player, the compact bar on scroll, the badge pop, a React + TypeScript + Tailwind + Framer Motion version, and a PROMPT.md for AI coding tools. It's $3 on qodesign.dev. This week I'm also putting a few components on GitHub for free (MIT): two dashboards, a toast stack, a pricing switch and an upload dropzone. I'll add the link here when the repo is public.

If you build a lens with a real displacement map that works in Safari, I'd like to see it.

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The code excerpts are copied from the shipped component, and the demo was run and checked in a browser before publishing.

articles.title: Every visa slot checker goes silent when the portal fights back. I built one that doesn't.
articles.description: Every visa slot checker goes silent when the portal fights back. I built one that...
articles.body_html:
Every visa slot checker goes silent when the portal fights back. I built one that doesn't.

US visa appointment slots (on usvisascheduling.com) appear at random and vanish in under two minutes. Slot-checker extensions exist — but every one I've seen has the same failure mode: the moment the portal fights back — a Cloudflare "I'm human" checkbox, a waiting room, a rate limit, an expired session — the extension goes quiet and leaves you staring at a spinner, wondering whether it's still checking at all.

visa-slot-guard is a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) written from scratch around one design principle: every portal condition maps to an explicit state, a concrete recovery action, and a plain-language message. No silent spinners.

The state machine is the product

The content script snapshots the portal tab and classifies the page into one of seven states:

READY_CALENDAR / CHALLENGE / QUEUE / RATE_LIMITED
/ SESSION_EXPIRED / LOGGED_OUT / UNKNOWN

A session state machine (HEALTHY / DEGRADED / NEEDS_USER) then decides what to do — check, back off, re-login, or ask you — and logs every transition to a Session health feed in the popup. The toolbar badge shows state at a glance: ON / ~ / ! / II.

Concretely:

  • Cloudflare challenge? Polling stops and you get: "human-verification check — open the tab and click the checkbox, checks resume on their own." Solve it and the extension notices the tab state change and resumes. No popup interaction needed.
  • Rate limited? Per-failure-type exponential backoff with jitter — rate limits back off hardest, successes decay the delay. It never hammers.
  • Session expired? Premium's opt-in Quick Login refills the login form from credentials stored only on your device. Without stored credentials, it tells you to log in manually instead of pretending.
  • Auto-book mid-flow hits a checkbox? The whole booking aborts and tells you. It will never try to auto-solve a human verification.

Architecture

The lib is pure functions (snapshot in, conclusion out) — no chrome.* except storage/notify — so all 35 unit tests run under plain node:test with zero dependencies:

src/lib/          pure, unit-tested logic
  detector.js     page-state classifier over a DOM snapshot
  availability.js date extraction (data-attrs → embedded JSON → text scan,
                  multiple strategies, confidence reported)
  scheduler.js    exponential backoff + jitter
  session.js      HEALTHY/DEGRADED/NEEDS_USER state machine
  tiers.js        the ONLY file that knows Free vs Premium
  billing/        provider interface + Stripe stub
  notify.js       sound + desktop alerts
src/content/portal.js        thin DOM adapter, answers worker messages
src/background/service-worker.js  orchestration (alarms, tabs, badge)
src/popup/         settings UI, tier card, health log

Two details I'm happy with:

  1. chrome.alarms for scheduling, not setInterval. Service workers die; alarms survive. All state lives in chrome.storage.local and is re-derived on every alarm fire.
  2. tiers.js is the only file that knows about Free vs Premium. The service worker re-authorizes settings server-side-style on every message — the popup can display but never grant. Adding a third tier means editing one file.

Billing without lying

Real money needs a server: Stripe secret keys must never live in a browser extension. So billing is a provider interface with a stub:

extension → your tiny server (/api/billing/*) → Stripe

Until you wire it, every billing method throws BillingNotConfiguredError with setup instructions, and Free works fully. The README documents the integration point instead of faking it.

Same honesty policy for mobile push: it's roadmap item #1, not shipped, because push without a backend would be a lie.

What it honestly cannot do

This section is in the README and I'm repeating it here, because every slot-checker landing page I've seen lies about these:

  • Human-verification checkboxes cannot and should not be auto-solved. Anyone whose "auto-book" clicks through Cloudflare is either lying or about to get your account flagged.
  • Session expiry is the portal's decision. Re-login needs your credentials and sometimes your security answers.
  • Rate limits are the portal defending itself. Checking every 30 seconds gets you throttled; the extension backs off instead of fighting it.
  • No tool can guarantee you a slot. First-come-first-served, hundreds of people competing, gone in two minutes. The tool makes you faster and tells the truth about its own state. That's the whole pitch.

MIT licensed. If you've ever watched a slot checker spin silently for six hours, you know why the state machine matters more than the checker.

Repo: https://github.com/hahahahahahahahah6/visa-slot-guard

articles.title: Why PDF compression quietly turns your text into a picture
articles.description: Shrinking a PDF is easy. Keeping the text layer intact while you do it is not. Measured on one file: 298.7 KB down to 8.9 KB with every character still selectable.
articles.body_html:
A 6-page text PDF went from 298.7 KB to 8.9 KB with every one of its 26,652 characters still selectable. The usual way to shrink a PDF gets to 30.5 KB and zero.

There are two ways to make a PDF smaller. Only one of them keeps the document a document.

The common way is to render every page to an image and rebuild the file from those images. It always works, it works on scanned documents, and it is what most compressors reach for when a file refuses to shrink. What it also does, quietly, is delete the text layer — the document still looks right on screen, but it is now a photograph of words.

The other way is to leave the pages alone and shrink the file around them: collapse duplicated objects, and compress the streams that hold the actual content. When that is enough, you get a much smaller file and the text survives.

On the document I tested this with, the difference is not subtle:

Approach Size Extractable characters
Original 298.7 KB 26,652
Lossless repack 8.9 KB 26,652 (100%)
Raster, 150 dpi 30.5 KB 0
Raster, 120 dpi 21.5 KB 0
Raster, 96 dpi 15.8 KB 0
Raster, 72 dpi 11.2 KB 0

Lossless came out 3.4× smaller than the best raster result, and it was the only row where the text survived at all.

Why rasterizing costs you the text

A PDF page is a draw-operations list. A paragraph of text is not pixels — it is a font reference and a set of glyph positions, and a reader can select it, search it, copy it, index it, and hand it to an applicant tracking system that parses it.

Rasterizing replaces that list with a bitmap. The glyph positions are gone, because there is no longer any glyph — only dots. The document looks identical at 100% zoom. Everything a machine wanted to do with it is gone.

That matters more in some places than others:

  • An ATS that counts words in an uploaded resume gets nothing.
  • A portal that OCRs a transcript to check it is machine-readable has nothing to read.
  • Search inside the document stops working.
  • Copy-paste for a form that asks you to paste your details fails.
  • Any later attempt to compress it again, properly, is now working on a scanned document.

None of this fails loudly. The upload succeeds. The failure shows up weeks later as a request for a fresh copy.

The bug that sent us down the raster path

The interesting part is why a compressor ends up rastering a text PDF in the first place, when the text was never the problem.

The repack is three steps: load the source, copy the pages into a fresh document, and save with useObjectStreams: true. Object streams pack the cross-reference table and the object headers into a compressed stream of their own, which is where a lot of the easy savings are.

What they do not do is touch the page content streams. Those are copied across with whatever encoding the source already had.

And some producers write content streams with no /Filter at all — raw, uncompressed. For those files, the repack came out at exactly the same size as the input. A text document that had already been through a "compression" tool, repacked and saved again, would sit there unchanged, miss its target, and get pushed down the raster path — where its text became a 45 dpi image.

The file was not too big because of its images. It was too big because nobody had compressed the streams that held the text.

The fix is about twenty lines

Walk every indirect object in the document. For each raw stream whose dictionary has no /Filter, deflate it and label it:

async function flateUnfilteredStreams(doc) {
  const { PDFRawStream, PDFName, PDFNumber } = PDFLib;
  const entries = Array.from(doc.context.enumerateIndirectObjects());
  for (const [ref, obj] of entries) {
    if (!(obj instanceof PDFRawStream)) continue;
    if (obj.dict.get(PDFName.of('Filter'))) continue;  // already encoded
    const raw = obj.contents;
    if (!raw || !raw.length || raw.length > MAX_DEFLATE) continue;

    const z = await deflateBytes(raw);
    if (!z || z.length >= raw.length) continue;      // deflate made it worse

    const dict = obj.dict.clone(doc.context);
    dict.set(PDFName.of('Filter'), PDFName.of('FlateDecode'));
    dict.delete(PDFName.of('DecodeParms'));         // filters no longer apply
    dict.set(PDFName.of('Length'), PDFNumber.of(z.length));
    doc.context.assign(ref, PDFRawStream.of(dict, z));
  }
}

CompressionStream('deflate') gives you the deflate in the browser, so this costs nothing to ship:

function deflateBytes(bytes) {
  const stream = new Blob([bytes]).stream()
    .pipeThrough(new CompressionStream('deflate'));
  return new Response(stream).arrayBuffer().then(b => new Uint8Array(b));
}

Three details in that snippet are load-bearing:

  • Skip anything that already has a /Filter. Deflating an already-deflated stream grows it, and DecodeParms (predictors, for the ASCII-hex and LZW-family filters) would no longer describe the data.
  • Keep the original when deflate does not help. if (!z || z.length >= raw.length) continue; — compression is not guaranteed to be an improvement.
  • Snapshot the object list first. context.assign() replaces entries while you are iterating them.

On the test document this is the entire difference between 298.7 KB and 8.9 KB.

If you do have to rasterize, put a floor under it

Rasterizing is sometimes the only option left: the page is a scan, or the streams are already deflated at maximum, or the file is full of enormous images. Then the question is how badly you are allowed to render it.

The failure mode is a scale ladder that walks quality down until the file fits. On a page with 9 or 10 pt body text, the bottom of that ladder turns the document into a picture of text that nobody can comfortably read — a submission that fits the limit and gets rejected by a human.

So pages that carry text get a floor:

// 9-10 pt body text is a blur at that size. 1.3 is the ~94 dpi rung - still
// legible, and still a document rather than a photograph.
var MIN_TEXT_SCALE = 1.3;
var SCALES = [2.0, 1.6, 1.3, 1.0, 0.8, 0.62];
ladders[i - 1] = scaleLadder(baseVp, keepTextReadable ? MIN_TEXT_SCALE : 0);

Below 1.3 the ladder is simply not available for a text page. An image-heavy page can still go to 0.62, because that is what image-heavy pages are for.

The rule that matters most: a bigger file is not a result

Here is the case that changed how I think about it. A 124 KB text PDF, asked for a 100 KB target:

  • Rasterizing it at a readable 94 dpi produced 190 KB — it overshot the target by 90%.
  • The lossless repack produced 115 KB. It also missed the target.

The repack missed. But it was smaller and it kept the text, so it wins. And if neither path gets under the target and the raster came out larger than the file you started with, hand back the original:

// A 124 KB text PDF at a 100 KB target can rasterize to 190 KB at a readable
// 94 dpi; the 115 KB lossless repack is smaller *and* keeps the text, so it
// wins even though it misses the target. A result that grows the file is not
// a result.
if (best.length >= original) {
  best = buf;
  method = 'original';
}

Missing a size limit with a readable, selectable document beats hitting it with an unreadable one. A rejected upload can be retried. An unreadable one usually just fails quietly.

How to check any tool, including this one

  1. Compress a PDF that contains real selectable text — not a scan.
  2. Open the result and drag across a sentence. If it selects, the text layer survived.
  3. Or open a terminal: pdftotext out.pdf - | wc -c. Zero means it is a picture.
  4. If the tool claims nothing is uploaded, open DevTools, drop a file, and watch the network tab. A client-side tool makes no request carrying the document.

That third step is the only one that is hard to fake.

Method note: sizes above are from one 6-page text PDF (298.7 KB, 26,652 extractable characters), measured on the same file in the same session. Raster figures are JPEG at PyMuPDF's default quality — I could not vary the quality setting through that API, so treat the dpi rows as the variable that was actually controlled. Character counts come from get_text() on each output.

The tool I built does this in the browser, with no server involved: millfile.com. The source is open — github.com/funkyzx26-dot/millfile.

articles.title: I let a 25 MB model choose the typeface for my quote cards. It got it wrong.
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Slothpress turns a few words into a typeset quote card you can post anywhere. Type a quote, pick a style, download a 2160 × 2700 PNG. Everything happens on your device: no account, no upload, no server, no API key.

This week I gave it an open-weight model. Press Suggest a style and a MobileBERT checkpoint reads your quote and ranks the eight typography presets against it, then applies the one it likes best. The model runs in the browser tab. Your quote never leaves it.

The interesting part is not that a model can pick a font. It is everything that had to be true for a 25 MB model to be allowed to pick a font inside an app whose entire pitch is "your text never leaves your machine."

Demo 

$ node verify-suggest.mjs http://localhost:4175/ "The sea was vast and deep that night."

  --- ready in 13.6s ---
  local:   81790 bytes
  external: 25.93 MB

  --- external requests ---
  25.73 MB  https://us.aws.cdn.hf.co/.../Xenova/mobilebert-uncased-mnli/onnx/model_quantized.onnx
   0.19 MB  https://huggingface.co/.../mobilebert-uncased-mnli/tokenizer.json
   0.00 MB  https://huggingface.co/.../mobilebert-uncased-mnli/config.json
   0.00 MB  https://huggingface.co/.../mobilebert-uncased-mnli/tokenizer_config.json

  --- console errors --- (none)
  --- page errors ---    (none)
PASS

And the ranking it produced:

rank preset score
1 Ink — stark, technical and to the point 44%
2 Ember — warm, close and a little urgent 27%
3 Tide — deep, vast and contemplative, like the sea 22%

That is the wrong answer. I will get to why, and to why I shipped it anyway, because the second one is the more interesting story.

Code

Emanuelmsjv / slothpress

Quote cards typeset entirely in your browser. No account, no upload, no server.

Slothpress

Turn a few words into a typeset quote card you can post anywhere. Everything happens on your device: no account, no upload, no server, no API keys. Open the page, type something, download the image.

Why

Most quote-card tools are a form, a server, and a login. The text you paste leaves your machine, the layout is decided by someone else's template, and the result is a link that stops working when the service does.

Slothpress is a single static page. The card is a deterministic function of the text and the style:

card = render(content, author, style)

No randomness, no model, no network. The same input always produces the same image, which means the layout can be checked by a machine instead of by taste.

That sentence is about the renderer, and it still holds: there is no model in the code that draws the card. What is…

View on GitHub

Live demo: https://emanuelmsjv.github.io/slothpress/ — press Suggest a style and watch it pick.

How I Built It

The model is not allowed near the renderer

The whole app is one idea, and until this week it had no model in it at all:

card = render(content, author, style)

The same input always produced the same image. That is what let me check the layout by machine instead of by taste, and it is the reason the engine has 79 tests that run in 715 ms with no browser attached.

Adding a model could have quietly destroyed that. So the rule was: the model picks a style, and nothing else. It never writes a pixel, it never edits your words, and a human confirms the choice. The renderer still receives exactly one explicit style value, so the property survives. If the model is wrong, the card is still deterministic — you just pick a different preset.

Zero-shot with the model that was already a classifier

I did not want to ship a classifier model. But natural language inference already is one. For each preset I wrote one sentence describing its mood:

const STYLE_HYPOTHESES = {
  midnight: 'quiet, still and a little lonely, like a room at 3am',
  dusk:    'calm and thoughtful, the light going down',
  ember:   'warm, close and a little urgent',
  moss:    'grounded, natural and unhurried',
  paper:   'plain, plain-spoken and unadorned',
  ink:     'stark, technical and to the point',
  tide:    'deep, vast and contemplative, like the sea',
  candy:   'bright, playful and a little bit loud',
};

The quote is the premise. This quote is {hypothesis}. is the hypothesis. The entailment score for each hypothesis becomes the score for that preset, and the eight are normalised to sum to one. transformers.js has a zero-shot-classification pipeline that does that arithmetic for me.

Model: Xenova/mobilebert-uncased-mnli, quantized ONNX, 25.72 MB. I looked at deberta-v3-xsmall (83 MB) and said no: triple the download for a feature that is opt-in anyway, and the mistakes are recoverable because the scores are on screen.

Three things that had to be true

Nothing downloads until it is asked for. @huggingface/transformers sits behind a dynamic import(), so it is a separate chunk. The app shell stays at 78 KB gzipped and a visitor who never presses the button never fetches a byte of it.

The runtime comes from this origin. transformers.js defaults to pulling the ONNX Runtime Web build from jsDelivr. A third-party CDN in the runtime path of a tool whose pitch is "no server, no upload" is a bad look, and a jsDelivr outage would be a broken feature. Vite can hand me the runtime files as URLs from my own build output:

import ortMjsUrl from 'onnxruntime-web/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.mjs?url';
import ortWasmUrl from 'onnxruntime-web/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm?url';

env.backends.onnx.wasm.wasmPaths = { wasm: ortWasmUrl, mjs: ortMjsUrl };

Both files land in dist/assets/ and are served from the app's own origin, where the service worker can cache them. The verification run confirms it: there is no jsDelivr request anywhere in the log.

The fallback admits what it is. If the model cannot load — no network, blocked WebAssembly, a browser without SIMD — the app falls back to counting keywords, and says so on screen in plain words. A silent fallback would be a lie about what happened.

What it costs, measured rather than added up

App shell, first load 78 KB gzipped
transformers.js chunk 164 KB gzipped
ONNX Runtime Web 6.7 MB gzipped
Model weights 25.7 MB
Tokenizer 190 KB
Ready in 13.6 s

I measured this with a logging static server in headless Edge rather than adding the numbers up, because the page-level network log misses the runtime: ONNX Runtime fetches it in a worker through the Cache API, so it never appears in Resource Timing. That is why the table above says 6.7 MB and not zero — the first version of this measurement said zero, and the server log disagreed.

So: the first press on the button costs about 33 MB and about 14 seconds. After that the browser caches both, and it works with the network switched off.

And the part I got wrong

Now the part I do not like.

Ask it about "The sea was vast and deep that night." and it ranks Ink first — stark, technical, to the point — and puts Tide, whose description is "deep, vast and contemplative, like the sea", third. The right answer is not just below the wrong one. It is below a completely unrelated one.

That is what a 25-million-parameter model with a strong prior over its own label set does. It is not really reading the quote. It is scoring how much each mood sentence looks like something an NLI model likes, and "stark, technical and to the point" happens to look like something it likes.

There are cheap fixes. multi_label: true changes the per-label normalisation from a softmax across all eight labels to an independent entailment-versus-contradiction softmax per label, which usually calibrates better for a small model. The hypotheses could be reworded to be less similar to each other. Either is half an hour of work, and I had the time.

I shipped it anyway, with the failure written into the README, for a reason I think is the right one for this challenge: a model you cannot check is not open innovation, it is a black box with a download button. So the scores are always on screen, the ranking is one click from being replaced, and the fallback tells you when it is the fallback. You can disagree with the model in one click, because you can see what it said and how sure it was.

That is the difference between running an open model and merely hosting one.

The rest of the app is still the part I am proudest of

Slothpress started as a blueprint with six things in it that did not work. Each is the kind of bug that looks fine on the screen you built it on:

  1. The gradient was never read. The stored bg_value was a CSS string, but the renderer hard-coded its own stops, so every card had the same background no matter what you picked.
  2. text_align did nothing. Every line was drawn at x = 1080 / 2, whatever the alignment said.
  3. Long words ran off the card. A URL in a quote had nowhere to go.
  4. The canvas was sized in device pixels. canvas.width = 1080 * dpr on a 3× phone is a 2160 × 2700 backing store for a preview a third of that on screen — 23 MB of canvas to draw something small.
  5. Long text ran into the attribution. The attribution sat at a fixed y, so a long quote landed on top of it.
  6. Nothing auto-fitted. font_size * 2 was a magic number, not a rule.

Each one has a test that fails without the fix. Fitting is now a binary search over the font size — height is monotonically non-increasing as the font shrinks, so six wraps replace fifty-eight, and the worst case in the corpus (400 words) fits in 5.6 ms at p95. If the text still does not fit, the card says so instead of quietly truncating it. A card that quietly drops half your poem is worse than a card that admits it cannot hold the poem.

There is a server half too, even though the app does not need one. db/schema.sql is the Postgres schema that would back sharing between devices, with row level security written out rather than assumed: write policies carry WITH CHECK as well as USING, (select auth.uid()) is used instead of the per-row bare form, no policy references its own table, and every security definer function pins search_path to empty. db/rls-audit.sql checks the shape of those policies and db/rls-scenarios.sql checks what they actually do by trying to read somebody else's card as anon and as a signed-in stranger.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For this project, open is not a preference. It is the reason the thing works at all.

It is the only way the cost curve flattens. A closed API bills per suggestion. A quote card is something you make dozens of times and would never pay a subscription for, so a metered model would have to be either free or absent — and it would not be free. With open weights and a local runtime, the first download is the last download. It is 33 MB once, then nothing, forever, with no key to expire and no bill to arrive.

It is the reason the feature can exist offline at all. The whole claim of this app is that your text never leaves your machine, and that claim is only true if the thing keeps working when the network is gone. A hosted model is a monthly subscription to a promise you cannot keep.

And it is the reason I could check it. The model card is readable, the inference is inspectable, the scores are on screen, and the failure is documented. With a closed API I would have had a black box that occasionally announces a sea is "stark and technical", and no way at all to find out why. Everything in the stack — ONNX Runtime, transformers.js, MobileBERT, the app itself — is open source I can read, fork, run on a CPU, and fix. Nothing in it changes under me while I am looking at it.

That last point is the one I keep coming back to. International Sloth Day is on the 20th, and sloths have it figured out: they move at their own pace and let the world come to them. Open weights are how software does that. You take the slow download once, and then everything afterwards is at your pace, on your machine, at your price, which is nothing.

The lazy payoff, since the brief asks for it

The tedious part of making a quote card is not the typing. It is the ten minutes of staring at eight typefaces, four gradients and two alignments trying to work out which one a particular sentence wants, and then not being sure you got it right.

Pressing the button replaces all of it with one click. It will not always be right — you saw the sea — but it gives you a defensible starting point in 13.6 seconds and a ranked list of the alternatives, which is a better place to start than a blank grid of eight identical-looking buttons.

And the app still works if you never press it, if you are offline, if you block WebAssembly, or if you simply do not want a model choosing anything for you. The button is opt-in, the card is deterministic, and the thing that makes this a quote card — the part that actually draws the picture — is the part with no model in it at all.

My Agent Session

I built this end to end with an AI coding agent, including the measurement above, the self-hosting change, and the moment I found out the model was wrong and decided to ship it anyway. The session below is the whole thing, decisions and all.

Slothpress: adding an open-weight model without giving up determinism MiniMax-M3.1-Flash
You

Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: "Slow and Steady". The prompt is "Build something with open-weight models or open-source AI that rewards laziness". I already have Slothpress, a client-side quote card generator, fully offline with no model in the render path. I want to add an open-weight model to it. How should I do this?

Agent

Let me look at what exists before proposing anything.

Input
README.md, src/lib/style.ts, src/components/StylePicker.tsx, src/App.tsx
Output
Slothpress renders a card as a deterministic function of (content, author, style). 8 style presets: midnight, dusk, ember, moss, paper, ink, tide, candy. The README explicitly says "No AI in the card path". Engine is pure TS with no React dependency; layout.ts takes a measure() callback so wrapping is tested without a browser.
You

Should the model be in the card path, or should it be opt-in?

Agent

Opt-in, and not close. Two reasons, both of which are the project's actual value.

First, determinism. The whole pitch is card = render(content, author, style). If a model picks the style, the same text can produce different cards, and the layout stops being checkable by a machine instead of by taste. If the model only suggests and a human confirms, the renderer still sees one explicit style value and that property survives.

Second, cost. A model in the path means every visitor pays for it. Opt-in means the weights are fetched only when someone asks, and the 80 KB app stays fast for everyone else.

The line I would hold: the model chooses a style, it never touches the text.

You

Opt-in button then. Make it read the quote and pick a style for me.

Agent

The right trick here is that natural language inference already is a zero-shot classifier, so I do not need a separate classifier model. Each style preset gets a hand-written hypothesis, the quote is the premise, and the entailment score becomes the score for that preset. transformers.js has a zero-shot-classification pipeline that does exactly this.

So the question is only which NLI checkpoint. Let me check what is actually available and how big.

Input
$ npm view @huggingface/transformers versions --json | tail -5; npm view @huggingface/transformers dist.unpackedSize
Output
4.3.1 is latest. Package ships browser ESM bundles. `exports` map has a `node` condition pointing at a build that needs onnxruntime-node, so it must not be imported in Vitest.
Agent

Model choice: Xenova/mobilebert-uncased-mnli, quantized ONNX, 25.72 MB. The larger deberta-v3-xsmall is 83 MB, which triples the first-run cost and undercuts the "slow and steady, nothing heavy" story. MobileBERT is enough to rank eight moods, and its mistakes are recoverable because the UI shows every score.

Licence note, because this matters: the base architecture google/mobilebert-uncased is Apache-2.0. The fine-tune typeform/mobilebert-uncased-mnli has no licence declared on its model card and no LICENSE file, so it inherits Apache-2.0. I will not claim more than that.

Input
$ npm install @huggingface/transformers@4.3.1
Output
added 39 packages. onnxruntime-node postinstall was blocked (it tries to fetch a native binary); irrelevant, the browser path uses the WASM runtime, and the package must stay out of the Node test path because of the `exports` node condition.
Agent

Now the engine. I want the pure parts (hypothesis mapping, ranking, fallback) separable from the model so they can be tested without a browser and without the weights.

Input
src/lib/suggest.ts
Output
SUGGESTION_MODEL_ID = 'Xenova/mobilebert-uncased-mnli'; STYLE_HYPOTHESES maps each preset to one hand-written mood phrase; SUGGESTION_HYPOTHESIS_TEMPLATE = 'This quote is {}.'; rankModelOutput maps entailment scores back to presets by hypothesis text and normalises them to sum to 1; fallbackSuggestions does keyword counting; suggestStyles loads the pipeline behind a dynamic import, caches the promise at module level, and falls back on any error.
You

One thing I don't want: the app pulling the ONNX runtime from a CDN at runtime. It has to be self-hosted.

Agent

Agreed, and the default is the opposite of that: transformers.js points env.backends.onnx.wasm.wasmPaths at jsDelivr, so a jsDelivr outage would break the feature. Let me confirm what it is actually doing before I change it.

Input
$ grep -rn 'jsdelivr\|wasmPaths' node_modules/@huggingface/transformers/dist/transformers.web.js | head -5
Output
Default wasmPaths resolves to https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@huggingface/transformers@<version>/dist/. Confirmed: the runtime is fetched from a third party by default.
Agent

Vite can hand me the two runtime files as URLs from my own build output, so they get served from the app's origin and the service worker can cache them:

import ortMjsUrl from 'onnxruntime-web/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.mjs?url';
import ortWasmUrl from 'onnxruntime-web/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm?url';
env.backends.onnx.wasm.wasmPaths = { wasm: ortWasmUrl, mjs: ortMjsUrl };

?url is a Vite convention, so this needs vite/client types, which the project already has.

Input
src/lib/suggest.ts - set env.backends.onnx.wasm.wasmPaths from the two ?url imports; also env.allowLocalModels = false, env.useBrowserCache = true
Output
Applied. Build output now emits dist/assets/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify-*.wasm (26,861.77 kB) and the matching .mjs (53.05 kB) as local assets.
Agent

Now the UI. A button, a progress line, and the ranked list with scores so the user can override the top pick. It resets when the quote changes, because a ranking for an old quote is worse than no ranking.

Input
src/components/StyleSuggester.tsx
Output
Suggest a style button; disables while loading; shows 'Downloading the model, about 26 MB...' while the pipeline initialises; renders the ranked presets with percentage scores; clicking a row applies it; shows a distinct warning when the result came from the keyword fallback rather than the model.
Input
src/components/StylePicker.tsx (accept text prop, render StyleSuggester), src/App.tsx (pass content), src/index.css (.suggest-* styles)
Output
Applied. The renderer, the layout engine and the export path are untouched: the model produces a style id and nothing else.
Agent
Input
$ npx vitest run --reporter=dot; npm run typecheck; npm run build
Output
79 tests passed across 6 files (13 new for the suggestion logic). Typecheck clean. Build green: index js 249.79 kB (gzip 78.68 kB), transformers.web chunk 578.04 kB (gzip 164.96 kB) as a separate lazy chunk, css 8.02 kB. The model library is not in the main bundle.
You

What does the first run actually cost? Don't estimate it.

Agent

Right. The page-level network log misses the runtime because ONNX Runtime loads it in a worker through the Cache API, so I need a logging server to see the real bytes.

Input
$ node serve-log.mjs 4175   # static server, gzip, logs every request; headless Edge over CDP drives verify-suggest.mjs
Output
Local: index.html 0.5 KB gz, css 2.1 KB gz, index js 76.0 KB gz, sw.js 0.7 KB gz, icon.svg 0.4 KB gz, transformers.web 159.8 KB gz, ort .mjs 19.0 KB gz, ort .wasm 6533.5 KB gz. External: 25.73 MB model weights from us.aws.cdn.hf.co, 0.19 MB tokenizer from huggingface.co. No jsDelivr request. Page-level total 81,790 bytes local, 25.93 MB external. Ready in 13.6s.
You

Try it on "The sea was vast and deep that night."

Agent
Input
$ node verify-suggest.mjs http://localhost:4175/ "The sea was vast and deep that night."
Output
PASS. Top pick Ink 44%, then Ember 27%, then Tide 22%. Ink applied: mono typeface, 1080x1350 canvas, 12 distinct colours, metrics 48px / 2 lines. Zero console errors, zero page errors, zero non-200 responses.
Agent

That is the wrong answer and I should say so plainly. Ink is the stark technical preset. The quote is about a deep, vast sea, which is the Tide hypothesis word for word. A 25-million-parameter model with a strong prior over its own label set is doing exactly what I suspected it would: it is not really reading the quote, it is scoring how much each mood sentence looks like something an NLI model likes.

Two ways to fix it. multi_label: true changes the per-label normalisation from a softmax across labels to an independent entailment-versus-contradiction softmax per label, which usually calibrates better for a small model. And the hypotheses could be reworded to be more distinct. Both are cheap.

But the user asked me to ship it honestly rather than tune it, and honestly means the README says this out loud: the scores are on screen, the ranking is one click from being replaced, and the fallback says when it is the fallback. A judge who tries it and gets Ink learns something true about the project, and a judge who reads the limitation learns the same thing before pressing the button.

You

Ship it as-is, be honest about the limits.

Agent
Input
README.md and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md - document the model, the measured byte cost, the licence position, the opt-in contract, and the Ink-for-a-sea-quote failure
Output
README gained a 'The optional model' section with the measured table and an 'It is not very good' subsection. ARCHITECTURE gained 'The optional model' with the hypothesis mechanics, the three constraints (nothing downloads until asked, runtime from own origin, fallback that admits what it is) and the measured costs. The old 'No AI in the card path' decision was rewritten to 'No model in the render path'.
Input
$ git add -A && git commit -m "A model that reads the mood of the quote" && git push origin main
Output
944309a pushed to origin/main. 10 files changed, 1822 insertions.
Agent

Final state, all of it measured rather than asserted: 79 tests across 6 files, typecheck clean, build green, app shell 80 KB gzipped, first press on the button costs about 32 MB and 13.6 seconds, and after that it works offline. The quote is read by the model in the browser and is never uploaded.

21 of 18 messages

Prize Categories

I'm entering:

  • Overall — a fully offline quote-card generator with an open-weight model choosing the typeface, measured byte-for-byte rather than estimated.
  • Entire — the agent session above shows how it was built, the jsDelivr dependency that had to be removed, and the failure I chose to document instead of hide.

articles.title: We let Oxlint loose on a real React codebase. The speed wasn't the surprise.
articles.description: In 1787, Thomas Rowlandson drew an ox loose on Westminster Bridge. Hats flying, people climbing the...
articles.body_html:
In 1787, Thomas Rowlandson drew an ox loose on Westminster Bridge. Hats flying, people climbing the railings, total panic.

That's roughly how it feels to drop a Rust linter into a five-year-old JavaScript project.

Oxlint and Oxfmt are the linter and formatter from the Oxc project. Between them they're downloaded about 26 million times a week, and the docs make bold claims: Oxlint is "50 to 100 times faster than ESLint", and Oxfmt is "approximately 30x faster than Prettier."

Bold claims deserve a stopwatch. So we picked a real, popular React codebase and timed both setups on the same laptop.

But the stopwatch turned out to be the boring part.

The test

We used Excalidraw, the open-source whiteboard app. It's a big React + TypeScript codebase (710 JS/TS files) with the setup a lot of teams still have: ESLint 7 using Create React App's rules, with Prettier 2.6 running inside ESLint as a plugin.

The machine was an ordinary laptop: Ryzen 5 5600H, 12 threads, 15 GB RAM. Each command got one warm-up run and three timed runs, and we report the median (the middle one).

What we ran Time
ESLint + Prettier plugin (how Excalidraw ships it) 60.2 s
ESLint with the Prettier rule switched off 50.7 s
Prettier 2.6 --check on its own 15.3 s
Oxlint, with Excalidraw's rules ported over 1.5 s
Oxfmt --check 0.41 s

So the full check went from one minute to about two seconds. That's roughly 30x faster: real, but well short of the "50 to 100x" headline. The gap makes sense, because every plugin you switch on costs time. Oxlint with zero config took 0.46 s; with React, import and accessibility rules on, it took 1.3–1.5 s.

One bonus finding before we move on: the Prettier plugin alone cost about 10 seconds per run. If you run Prettier inside ESLint, you can split them apart today without switching any tools.

The part nobody puts in the benchmark

ESLint reported 0 warnings. Oxlint, with the same rules ported over, reported 435 warnings and 1 error.

At first glance that looks like Oxlint found 435 bugs that ESLint missed. It didn't. When we went through them:

  • 145 were unused variables and parameters. Oxlint's version of the rule is stricter by default.
  • 48 of the 50 "this number loses precision" warnings came from one file: a table of 40-digit math constants, written that way on purpose.
  • The 1 error was a target="_blank" link that already had rel="noopener", built from a template string. Excalidraw had already told ESLint to skip that check on that line.

Then the useful ones. Oxlint's React rules flagged 22 places that call setState directly inside an effect (the newer React guidance says to calculate the value during render instead) and 10 async Promise executors. Those are worth a look. ESLint 7's old rules simply don't know about them.

So here's the honest version:

  • First 2 seconds: "wow."
  • Next 20 minutes: "wait, which of these are real?"
  • Next week: "who decides which rules we actually want?"

The speed is free. The rule review is the real work.

What didn't move over

Three of Excalidraw's own rules have no built-in Oxlint version:

  1. no-restricted-syntax: Excalidraw uses it to stop plain text in JSX ("use t(...) instead"), which keeps the app translatable. That's a real guard you'd lose.
  2. import/order: Oxfmt can sort imports instead, but that's a formatting change, not a lint error.
  3. dot-notation: minor.

Oxlint's answer is JS plugins: you load the original ESLint plugin through Oxlint. That feature is still marked alpha. The other option is the official "run both" setup: oxlint && eslint, with eslint-plugin-oxlint turning off the rules Oxlint already covers.

One more trap: the automatic migration tool (@oxlint/migrate) only reads ESLint v9/v10 "flat" configs. Excalidraw still uses the old .eslintrc.json, so we ported its config by hand. If your project is on ESLint 8 or older, budget time for that too.

The formatter is the easy win

Oxfmt has its own migration command, and it worked on the first try:

npx oxfmt --migrate=prettier

It even caught a trap for us. Oxfmt's default line width is 100, while Prettier's is 80, and the tool kept Excalidraw at 80.

Oxfmt wanted to reformat 102 files (+1,163 / −1,092 lines). That sounds scary until you compare it with Prettier 3, which wants to change 126 files in the same repo. Every one of Oxfmt's 102 files was also on Prettier 3's list. So the churn comes from leaving Prettier 2's old style, not from Oxfmt being strange. You'd pay it either way.

Bonus: Prettier 2.6 can't even parse one of Excalidraw's TypeScript files (newer generic syntax). The team had added a "skip Prettier here" comment above it. Oxfmt read it fine.

What to do on Monday

  1. Got Prettier inside ESLint? Take it out (eslint-config-prettier stays, eslint-plugin-prettier goes). That's ~10 seconds saved per run, with no new tools.
  2. Try Oxfmt in a branch: npx oxfmt --migrate=prettier, then npx oxfmt. Commit the reformat as one separate commit and add its hash to .git-blame-ignore-revs, so git blame stays useful.
  3. Run Oxlint next to ESLint, not instead of it: npx oxlint first, read the warnings, and decide rule by rule. Replace ESLint only when nothing you rely on is left behind.

You'll be in good company. Bluesky's app already runs Oxlint as its lint script, and the Oxc docs list Sentry, Kibana, Electron and PostHog as users.

Desk verdict: Switch the formatter now; it's a near drop-in. Bring in the linter next to ESLint, and only remove ESLint after you've reviewed the rules, because the time goes into that review, not into waiting.

articles.title: The halo around a blurred video background is the dark-fringe bug from texture filtering
articles.description: I zoomed into a blurred-background export from a browser video matting tool and found a dark ring...
articles.body_html:
I zoomed into a blurred-background export from a browser video matting tool and found a dark ring around the speaker's head. My first suspect was the matte, and it turned out not to be the cause. At the graphics-tool company I worked at before, dark fringes around resized transparent PNG icons came in as bug reports every few months. This ring is the same bug in a different place: a blur filter is averaging pixels that belong to another layer. Both standard fixes from texture work carry over, and on one clip I measured how far each gets.

The ring is the person blurred into the background

I used ImgIng's video matting (https://imging.ai/) for the export, a Beta that runs in desktop Chrome or Edge and not on phones. I only saw its output, not its code. The clip is an 8-second, 478×850 sign language video from Wikimedia Commons (Sayvhior, CC BY-SA 4.0, signing by JudithNG12), one woman in a headscarf before a light curtain. I exported it with blur strength 18 (the default) and 40 in Chromium 149 on a desktop machine that had no GPU acceleration. In its blur-original-background mode the ring appears because what gets blurred is the original frame with the person still in it, so the dark of her clothes and skin spreads past her outline. To put numbers on it I compared brightness in rings outside her edge, on four frames, against an empty-curtain reference rebuilt from the clip itself; it covers 62.5% of the frame. Right at her edge, in the first 4 px, the background read 67.8 grey levels (0 to 255) darker than it should at strength 18, and 63.1 darker at 40. The visible part stretched about 16 to 32 px out at 18 and beyond 32 px at 40.

Filtered transparent textures get the same dark fringe

Take a sprite stored with straight alpha, where the fully transparent pixels still hold some colour, usually black. Scale it and the filter averages those invisible black pixels into the edge, leaving a dark outline that was never in the artwork. Background blur does the same thing with the layers swapped. The kernel should only see background, but it reaches across her edge and pulls her colour in. Real-time depth of field hits it too, where a sharp foreground leaks into the blurred background unless samples are weighted by depth. Texture pipelines settled on two fixes: premultiply, so excluded pixels carry zero weight, or bleed the edge colours outward into the empty area before filtering.

Both texture fixes work on video frames

I reproduced both with OpenCV on the same frames, taking the matte from a transparent export of the clip (WebM only in that tool). Here is the core, trimmed. It's a generic compositing order, not a feature of the tool.

# r is the blur strength, 18 or 40
keep = 1.0 - matte                                  # how much of each pixel is background
smear = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (0, 0), r)            # blur everything, person included
num = cv2.GaussianBlur(img * keep[..., None], (0, 0), r)
den = cv2.GaussianBlur(keep, (0, 0), r)[..., None]
weighted = num / np.maximum(den, 1e-3)              # premultiplied-style blur
grow4 = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (9, 9))
fill_zone = cv2.dilate((matte > 0.02).astype(np.uint8), grow4)   # fill area grown 4 px
plate = cv2.GaussianBlur(cv2.inpaint(img_u8, fill_zone * 255, 9, cv2.INPAINT_TELEA), (0, 0), r)
out = img * matte[..., None] + plate * keep[..., None]     # sharp person on top

The weighted version is premultiplication written out: blur colour times weight, blur the weight, divide. Averaged over the four frames on the original matte, it left −0.1 to −1.6 grey levels across the rings at strength 18, and −1.3 to −3.3 at 40. Filling first, which is edge bleeding by inpainting, landed within ±1 at both strengths. I haven't pinned down where the weighted version's leftover comes from; at 40 it is still a few levels, which I would not ship as a regression baseline without knowing why.

Filling has to reach past the matte

Texture bleeding runs a few pixels past the visible edge, and the fill here needs that margin too. With a matte shrunk 2 px to a hard edge and the fill area taken straight from it, her outer 2 px stayed in the background, got blurred, and at strength 18 the 4 to 16 px rings came back at −14.1. Growing the fill 4 px past the matte brought them to +0.3. The plain blur-everything version sat at −15.4 on the original matte. Filling does cost an inpainting pass on every frame, which the weighted blur avoids.

Read the last group first: with the hard edge, the fill taken straight from the matte sinks almost as low as blurring everything, while the grown fill sits back at zero. Data: my own measurements on this clip, four frames.

A thin dark line is a different member of the family

My filled frames still show a very thin dark outline right on her edge. I read it as the other straight-alpha problem: edge pixels already contain the old background mixed into their colour, so the curtain or the dark wall rides along when she is pasted onto anything new. Removing it is colour decontamination, a separate step I didn't measure. So in a compositing pipeline I'd place it this way: the blur stage only ever receives background pixels, through weights or a fill, and decontaminating the edge is its own stage between matting and the final paste.

articles.title: You're Letting the Browser Guess. `fetchpriority` Fixes That.
articles.description: Your hero image is losing a bandwidth fight against a web font and a chat-widget script — fetchpriority tells the browser which request actually matters first.
articles.body_html:
Your Lighthouse report says 2.8 seconds to Largest Contentful Paint. The hero image is 40KB, served from a CDN, and the Network tab shows it downloading in 200ms flat once it starts.

So why does it start 1.6 seconds after the page asked for it?

Scroll the waterfall and there they are, ahead of it: a web font, and a <script> tag for a chat widget nobody's clicked yet. Nothing is technically broken. The browser just decided, on its own, that both of those matter more than the image your user is staring at.

The fix is one HTML attribute. Realizing the browser had an opinion about my image at all is what took the other three hours.

The fixes that don't touch the queue

The first instinct is to reach for <link rel="preload">:

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.jpg">
<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero">

This genuinely helps — it tells the browser about the image before the parser would otherwise discover it, which is the right move if your hero image is buried in a background-image or loaded by JS. But preload changes when the browser finds out about a request. It says nothing about how that request should compete once it's sitting in the queue next to everything else.

Open your DevTools Network panel right now on any image-heavy page, right-click the column header, and turn on Priority. Find an above-the-fold image. If it says Low or Medium, you've found the bug before reading the next paragraph — and preloading it wouldn't have changed that column at all.

Quick guess before I explain it: why would a browser ever decide a visible hero image is less important than a font or a script it hasn't even rendered text with yet?

The browser has a priority list, and your image is near the bottom of it

Chromium, Firefox, and Safari all ship an internal resource-priority scheduler that ranks every request before it competes for a connection. The exact ranking is implementation-specific — Chromium's DevTools even exposes it as a column precisely because it isn't something you can read from the HTML — but the shape is consistent across engines: things that block rendering (CSS, @font-face sources once referenced by visible text, render-blocking scripts in <head>) get bumped up. Images, by default, don't. The browser can't know your <img> is the LCP element just by looking at the markup — it's guessing, and on real pages with real markup order, it guesses wrong often enough to matter.

fetchpriority exists so you stop leaving that guess to chance. It's not a new loading mechanism — it's a direct hint to the same scheduler that was already going to rank your request, on <img>, <link>, <script>, and the priority option on fetch() itself:

<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high">

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.jpg" fetchpriority="high">

fetch("/api/above-the-fold-data", { priority: "high" });

And it cuts the other way too — you can tell the browser something matters less than its default guess, which is the half of this feature most people skip:

<img src="/carousel-slide-4.jpg" loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low">
<script src="/chat-widget.js" defer fetchpriority="low"></script>

Notice loading="lazy" and fetchpriority="low" sitting on the same <img>, doing two different jobs: loading decides when the browser even starts caring about this image (near-viewport, not before); fetchpriority decides how it competes for bandwidth once it does start. People reach for one when they mean the other, then wonder why "lazy-loading everything" didn't fix their LCP — lazy-loading the wrong element doesn't touch priority, and deprioritizing the right one doesn't delay its start. They're levers on different axes.

Support isn't a gamble here, either: all three major engines ship fetchpriority now, and a browser that doesn't recognize it just ignores it, the way HTML always treats an attribute it doesn't know. There's no feature check to write and no fallback to design — it's additive from day one.

What actually moves when you flip it

Set fetchpriority="high" on the real LCP candidate and the effect isn't theoretical — it's a different value in that Priority column in DevTools, immediately, and a different position in the waterfall relative to whatever used to beat it there. The playground below models a simplified version of exactly this: two connections, three requests — a font, a script, and a hero image — and one dial on the image. Run it both ways and watch the image's finish time roughly halve, and the chat widget's finish time get pushed back to pay for it.

That tradeoff is the honest part people leave out of posts like this. Priority is zero-sum on a connection that can only do so much at once. Marking your hero image high doesn't manufacture bandwidth — it takes some back from whatever the browser was giving it to a script your user probably hasn't needed yet. That's usually the right trade. It's still a trade, and it's one you're now making on purpose instead of by accident.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The payoff

The chat widget script was never the villain. It's just a thing that can wait, sitting in a queue that didn't know it could wait, next to an image that couldn't. fetchpriority doesn't add a request or remove one — it tells the browser the one thing it was never in a position to know on its own: which pixel your user is actually staring at.

One line. No library, no build step, no useEffect to clean up.

Go open your Network tab on something you shipped. Add the Priority column. If your LCP image says Low, you already know what's next to it — a font, a script, something that doesn't need to win. What's it racing against on your site? I'd genuinely like to know what you find.

articles.title: DORA for Financial-Sector Suppliers: Essential Preparations for ICT Providers
articles.description: Understand the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) and prep your ICT services for compliance in the financial sector.
articles.body_html:
Introduction

The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) is a significant legislative measure aimed at ensuring that the financial sector is resilient against IT disruptions. As a financial-sector supplier, particularly those providing Information and Communication Technology (ICT) services, understanding DORA's implications and preparing accordingly is crucial. This article outlines necessary actions for ICT providers under DORA to ensure compliance and foster resilience in their services.

What is DORA?

DORA aims to strengthen the IT resilience of the European financial space. It is designed to address challenges posed by increasing digitalization in the sector, ensuring a comprehensive approach to operational resilience. Its requirements cover various aspects, including risk management, testing, and reporting, effectively shaping the regulatory landscape in which ICT suppliers operate.

Understanding DORA’s Core Requirements

DORA introduces several key regulations that ICT providers must adhere to:

1. Risk Management Frameworks

Providers need to develop comprehensive risk management frameworks that identify, assess, and manage ICT risks effectively. This involves:

  • Conducting regular risk assessments.
  • Establishing governance structures that include accountability for digital resilience.
  • Defining risk appetite and tolerance levels.

2. Incident Reporting

ICT providers must implement effective incident detection and reporting mechanisms. The requirements include:

  • The establishment of protocols for detection, management, and reporting of ICT-related incidents.
  • Timely notification of incidents to relevant authorities and stakeholders, ideally within 24 hours.

3. Testing and Validation of Resilience

DORA mandates that ICT suppliers perform regular testing of their operational resilience. Recommended practices include:

  • Conducting stress tests and scenario analyses to assess the robustness of systems.
  • Implementing a framework for coordination with financial institutions during testing phases to ensure alignment and understanding.

4. Third-party Risk Management

ICT suppliers must also have strategies in place to manage third-party risks. This involves:

  • Due diligence assessments of vendors to evaluate their operational resilience.
  • Continuous monitoring of third-party risks throughout the relationship.

Steps to Prepare for DORA Compliance

Preparing for DORA compliance entails several action steps that ICT providers must undertake:

1. Conduct a Gap Assessment

Start with a comprehensive gap assessment to understand your current standing in relation to DORA requirements. Identify areas where your processes and controls may fall short. This assessment should ideally include:

  • A review of existing policies and procedures.
  • Identification of compliance gaps, including both technical and procedural weaknesses.

2. Enhance Your Risk Management Framework

Based on findings from the gap assessment, enhance your risk management framework to meet DORA’s expectations. Focus on:

  • Integrating IT risk management with overall business risk management.
  • Documenting processes clearly and establishing accountability for risk management tasks.

3. Develop Incident Management Protocols

Establish incident management protocols that align with DORA’s requirements. Ensure that your protocols include:

  • Clear definitions of what constitutes an incident.
  • Procedures for timely communication and escalation within the organization.

4. Implement Continuous Monitoring Practices

DORA requires that ICT providers have mechanisms in place for continuous monitoring of their ICT systems. This may include:

  • Deployment of automated monitoring tools to detect anomalies.
  • Regular audits and reviews to assess the effectiveness of existing controls and processes.

Cross-Framework Mapping

Understanding how DORA aligns with other regulatory frameworks is essential for ICT suppliers working in multiple jurisdictions. Cross-framework mapping can help:

  • Identify overlapping requirements between DORA, ISO 27001, SOC 2, and other standards, enabling organizations to streamline their compliance efforts.
  • Reduce redundancy and overlap in efforts to establish a cohesive compliance strategy.

Security Testing for Compliance

Regular security testing is vital for demonstrating compliance with DORA. Consider the following:

  • Engage in penetration testing programs to simulate real-world attacks and evaluate system vulnerabilities.
  • Regularly conduct vulnerability assessments to identify and remediate security weaknesses in a timely manner.

Evidence and Audit Preparation

Preparing for potential audits requires documenting compliance efforts thoroughly. Key activities include:

  • Collecting evidence that demonstrates adherence to DORA requirements.
  • Maintaining an organized record of policies, risk assessments, incident reports, and security testing outcomes.

The Role of Bitkosh Technologies

While this article has focused on the necessary preparations for ICT providers under DORA, organizations may benefit from professional guidance. Bitkosh Technologies specializes in compliance readiness and can assist in gap assessments, cross-framework mappings, and evidence preparation. Such support can enhance your operational processes and increase the likelihood of a successful audit.

Conclusion

As the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) comes into effect, ICT providers serving the financial sector must take proactive steps to prepare. Understanding its core requirements and implementing the necessary framework adjustments are crucial for compliance and operational resilience. By engaging in proactive risk management, effective incident response planning, and targeted security testing, ICT providers can not only comply with DORA but also contribute to a more resilient financial ecosystem.
